LORD DERBY ON THE LABOUR
QUESTION.

Nov one of our leading statesmen has caught
the ear of the general public so approvingly
as Lord DERBY. It has become quite a
fashion to praise whatever he utters, and as
a rule—though many may grumble at his
ingenious and careful balancing of pros and
eons., and his scientifid calculations as to action
and re-action in human affairs—nobody can
find fault with the passionless impartiality with
Which he arrives at his conclusions. His
is the candour described so well by CAN-
NING.—.

Too nice to praise by wholesale, or to blame,
Convinced that all men's motives are the same;
And finds, with keen, discriminating sight,
Black's not so black, nor white so very white.
And yet, a close examination of what he
occasionally utters betrays, not, perhaps, a
conscious leaning to his own side, but a lean-
, ing, nevertheless, so decided, that the accept-
ance of his opinions on public questions,
especially such as working men are in-
terested in, would be a most undesirable
• thing. His speech at the agricultural dinner at
Bury the other day is a little out of date as
matter for newspaper comment; but the
• points raised by him there in regard to the
labour question, will not be out of date for
a very long time yet; and, therefore, will bear
that kind of examination due to subjects of
permanent interest.
We cannot say that working men are much
Indebted to Earl DERBY for his admission of
their right to get the highest price they can
for their labour. There is not much novelty
in the statement that if any set of men "saw
their way to an extra two, three, or four
shillings a week more wages, or what was
the same thing, a reduction of hours without
a reduction of wages, it was not reasonable
to expect them to give up their chance
of scouring this, simply from specula-
tive considerations, or because they were
going to ruin trade in the long run, or
industry in general." Nor are we much
enlightened by the statement that, if half a
million of workmen were suddenly added to
the present working population, we should
not "hear much more of strikes or demands
or advanced wages." When it rains we get
Wet if we do not keep within doors, and. when
the anil ja out and the sky clear, umbrellas are
not greatly needed. His practical argument,
however, is that as there is no certainty the
present comparative scarcity of labour will
continue," those who have the command of
the market now in their hands, would do well
to use their power with moderation."
Nobody can object to advice like this, nor

what is meant by a market settling "down one
way or another," we really cannot tell in the
absence of some kind of explanation.
So far as the labour question is concerned,
this speech of Earl DERBY'S may be safely left
to the common-sense of our working people.
They will not put themselves into a glow of
enthusiasm about it, like our newspaper writers,
as they know how utterly hollow such plati-
tudes are; how absolutely meaningless as
applied to the active industry of the country.
But there is in this speech something besides
the labour question to which the attention of
the public ought to be drawn, because, as the
utterance of a man enjoying the reputation of
a statesman, nothing can be gathered from
it in regard to the future of the country calcu-
lated to beget anything but humiliation and
despair.
The passage already quoted as to working
men not giving up a trade advantage on
"speculative considerations, or because they
were going to ruin trade in the long run, or
industry in general," concludes thus :—" They
would naturally do the best for themselves,
and so would the masters in their place." Is
this a doctrine that can be applied to the lives
of men? Is it a social verity necessary to be
understood and practised in the poliey of a
nation? Does the Church pursue its mission
for what it can get ?—and can its points of
belief, its moral requirements, and its lofty
professions mean only loaves and fishes ?-
Are our soldiers and our sailors persons
who do their duty for easy service, a whole
skin, and full pay? , Are our statesmen and
law-makers only self-seekers, not caring what
becomes of the country in the future if they
can turn their schemings and struggles to pre-
sent private account? If this be the case, then
the working men are doing right when they
force from employers the uttermost penny they
can get, careless as to what evil consequences
may ensue to the country. And then, too, may
employers without reproach or blame press
to the earth and despoil without mercy the
poor wretches who have no resource but to
submit and die.

Facts justify much in this direction, bat
had as things are, we have not got far enough
in our downward course as a nation to accept
such a gospel as this. Men try to do the
best they can for themselves, but not in
entire oblivion of duty. In all our professions
—the Church, the medical, legal, and mili-
tary—there are men who look beyond their fees'
and their ease; and amongst our working
men, as amongst all other classes, thoughts
for the welfare of trade and the welfare of the
country generally, do arise when they are
considering their own interests; and, notwith-
standing, the high authority of Earl DERBY,
the country will still cling to the belief, how-
ever slowly it may approach a full realiza-
tion of the practice, that the welfare of the
citizen is best promoted and preserved by a
full consideration of what is best for the
welfare and progress of the nation.
There is no objection to the fairness and
impartiality of Lord DEBBY, but we can do
without his platitudes and his dignified
prosing on undignified common-places ; and
above all things, we can dispense with a gospel
of selfish greed, which appears to be uttered
because it finds a ready echo in the minds of
those who consider it the prime duty of man
on earth to look after "number one."

STANDING ARMIES AND THE GATHERING OF

TUE EAGLES.
Tun costliness of standing armies, to which
my remarks ,in last week's BEE-HIVE princi-
pally referred, is a serious question, and at
the present day it is unfortunately almost the
only aspect of this important subject which the
public can be brought to consider. A study
of history, however, will show that our an-
cestors regarded the effect which a standing
army has on the liberty of the nation as a
more important question even than that of its -
cost. What troubled England in the 17th
century, and what oppresses Europe now
more seriously than is generally supposed, is
the burthensome deadweight of such organi-
zations crushing down all civilizing agencies,
and keeping back the forces designed for the
shaping of new and happier times. All
counted, there cannot be fewer than four
millions of trainel men in the several armies
of Europe; and these men, though during
actual war at the service of the States to which
they belong, are also, it must be remembered,
at the service of their various Governments to
suppress at any time the growth of popular
thought, or to trample down all patriotic
efforts to enlarge the bounds of freedom or
advance the progress of mankind.

So jealous have Englishmen always been. on
this point that a standing:army was never re-
garded in England other*ise than with strong
disfavour, and at certain periods with even
deadly hostility. What Cir.int.Es I. paid
for his attempts to keep up a standing
army everybody knows. The famous Bill of
Rights passed shortly after the accession of
WlLListm and MARY to the British Throne
contains these memorable words :—" That
the raising or keeping astanding army
within the kingdom in the time of peace,
unless it be with the consent of Parliament,
is against the law." So necessary have our
rulers found it to abide by this constitutional
declaration, that the number of troops to be
maintained every year is determined by the
Cabinet and Parliament, and although it is
understood that a standing army will be
maintained as a matter of course, yet Parlia-
ment can nevertheless reduce it, or even
extinguish it any year by a simple majority
vote.

These precautions were devised in view of
the danger of a standing army to public
liberty, and now that the numbers of standing
armies are almost everywhere increasing,
and two mighty principles—the monarchical
and the democratic—are nearly everywhere
struggling for mastery, is it net time that all
men who in their hearts are on the side of
liberty and progress, should turn their thoughts
to the reducing and controlling of this dan-
gerous force, now almost absolutely at the
exclusive disposal of emperors and kings?
Whilst I write this the Emperors of a EnILANY,
AUSTRIA., and Russrl—the three men of all
others most interested in the destruction of
popular liberty—are in conclave. Who can
tell what they are plotting? They bold- in
their hands a military force of nearly two
millions of armed men, and wherever thev
may jointly agree to launch that force, every-
thing must fall crushed before it! What is
there on the continent of Europe to resist
this ? Where can we see the potency of
living principles in the hearts of nun which
would be the best saroguard agaiust such a

2 '

catastrophe? The danger is imminent—the
nrystery in which it is shrouded is profound
and impenetrable. We, as a nation, have to
keep up a huge standing army because we
are in the presence of this shameful danger,
or rather because the eondition of things
which has given rise to it is everywhere
around us. We cannot believe that a British
Government would give countenance or aid to
a Royal conspiracy, though we can suppose
British Governments capable of making very
base compromises under despotio preisures.
Our danger, of whatever kind it may be, is
remote, and we have time in which to work
for the purpose of averting it; not, however,
by the organization of great armies, but by
defining and carrying out great principles. We
can make dear the importance of international
friendliness—we can demonstrate the wealth,
creating power of unrestricted commerce pur-
sued in peace—we can put before the world
in letters of light the lesson how humanizing,
how enriching, hew elevating is freedom of
thought—how valuable is popular liberty—
and how safe for nations a sound political
enfranchisement may be. made. Let us leave,
then, to foreign government? and their op-
pressed subjects, plottings and plannings,
intrigues and conspiracies, debates and
decisions with closed doors, whether for the
people or against the people. Principles are
not propagated in the dark; high policies
cannot be pursued in secret. Whatever con-
cerns men's interests in a benefielal sense must
be done out in the open light of day that all
may see and approve and imitate. It is for
us, therefore, not to engage ourselves in foreign
entanglements. It is for us to prove by our laws,
and if necessary by our lives, that the hundreds
of millions spent every year by emperors and
kings for the supprt of armies are worse than
wasted—would be better parted with if flung
into the deepest caverns covered by the sea!
If this spirit were exhibited throughout
England—if its value were recognized by our
public men—if the masses of ou'r people would
insist on it in our national policy—if English-
men of all grades, especially working men,
would make it a conspicuous article of the ir
political creed, the working men of other
nations, profiting by such an example, would,
I am convinced, accept this new and true
faith in humanity, and the brute material of
great armies would come to comprehend hu-
man rights and human duties, and the rude
material of, such armies being thus changed,
emperors and kings would find out that there
Was in the world higher work for men to do
than that of fighting and butchering each
other.

If oar working people will insist on policies
of peace and seek to perfect the relations of
industry, we shall soon see changes in Europe
profitable even for emperors and kings, because
profitable for all men who can benefit them-
selves by pursuing honourably the nobler aims
of life.
But to secure this end the doors of Parlia-
ment should be effectively opened to working
men. Their ideas, uttered from so high a
platform, would enlighten and solidify the
thought of their class, and as the true interest
of the masses of the people must at all times
be the truest interest of the nation—in fact of
all nations—there would then be reason to hope
for a more speedy advent of brighter and more
prosperous and better days for all, than could
ever be brought about by " Standing
Armies."

" The hoarse dull drum would sleep, and man be
happy yet."

R. MATI§DEN LATITAIt,
President of the Labour -
Representation League.

MR. ARCHIBALD BRIGGS AND
TRADES' UNIONISIL

Tun chief part :of what Mr. AILOITIBILD
BRIGGS thought proper to trouble you with
last week was unnecessary. I have no quarrel
with that gentleman as the manager of the
Methley and Whitwood collieries. In that
capacity 1 accord to him all necessary power
to discharge any person—unionist or non-
unionist—who interferes injuriously Nvith the
work he has in hand. If any man in his
employment, under any pretext whatever,
"persecutes".. others, let that man be dis-
missed as a punishment for his wrong-doing,

or if men indulge in drunkenness when they
ought to be engaged in their work, Mr.
Bufaos has a perfect right to protect the in-
terests of his company by refusing to con-
tinue such persons in his employment. Nay,
further than this, the right of Mr. BRIGGS
•to
wage war with the Colliers' Union has not
been disputed; only so far as such a war is
carried on in the name of co-operation.
Mon have their prejudices, and, as a rule,
it is useless to 'argue against them. Imperfect
sympathies or strong antipathies are seldom
put right by logic, and that ARCHIBALD
BRIGGS is a monomaniac in his hatred of
trades unionism, nobody can fail to see who
reads his letter of last Saturday, in connection
with his previous action in this business.
Every paragraph of his letter is impregnated
with this feeling. It oozes out in every sen-
tence. It is not a sustained argument, it is
a continuous scream, which has been ringing
in our ears for as many years as we can
remember. Ho tells us he desires to make the
colliers " withdraw from unions against their
masters to be more thoroughly in union with
them," an excellent olject it' trades unions
have this meaning chiefly or in any strong
way. Ile says he finds the "unions
directly assailing" them, and observes that
non-union men, that "they may lead a quiet
life, and escape from being blackguarded and
dubbed blaoksheep, arc driven against their
convictions to subscribe to union funds," and
adds that their best men are insulted by union
men for working too hard." 'When he tells
us that non-union men who persecute others
shall quit their employment, Mr. BRIGGS
being, in such cases, the judge, we have a
pretty correct idea how justice will be ad
ministered, and against whom the charge of
persecution is most likely to lie. And when,
above all things, we are informed that the
company, "with the view of taking away
from our men the only justifiable reason which
• they have for being members of the union, are
going to establish a benefit fund in connection
with the collieries," and to subscribe a hand-
some amount for that purpose, we see pretty
clearly how intense the hatred of' Mr. Brans
and his friends is when they furnish so low
and contemptible a motive for an act in itself
so excellent and praiseworthy. To establish
a benefit fund, not because they came of
themselves to see its desirableness, but that it
may damage or destroy that which the men
had already established for themselves is so
obviously doing good in a spirit of mischief
that the merit of the act disappears in the
meanness of the motive.
But with a dislike to unionism even so
marked as that of Mr. BRIM; we should not
interfere, although for his own sake we should
regret it. A" good hater" is not the most con-
temptible or censurable of men. What we objeet
to is that he should seek to work out his hatred
in the name of co-operation, and what we toll
Mr. BRIGGS is, that co-operation has nothing
whatever to do with the question. If he has
entered into a fight with the Colliers' Union it
is`not because he is a co-operator, and perhaps
he may see this when ho reflects that before
he took upon himself that name he was fiercely
busy in this same quarrel, and even though
he himself stood square with his own con-
science on this ground, we are by no means
sure that this thing which he calls co-opera-
tion, and Nihickho manages at Whitwood and.
Methley, deserves to go by that name. When
ho threatened to withhold a bonus which
working men had earned under their agree-
ment with him, he wai not talking like a co-
operator, and when he and his shareholders
escaped from the diegrace_of such an act, and
contented themselves with taking the bonus
from the men who attended the Leeds meeting
for the incoming year, they certainly noted
more like persons vindictively bent on punish-
ing an act they disapproved, rather than like
temperate and just men seeking to attain a
necessary end by
..strictness and severity of
discipline.

This reward and punishment by giving or
withholding bonus is new in co-operation, and
we hope it, will confine itself to the collieries
of the Niessrs. BRIGGS, as we are sure that if
it works itself out into the general practice of
the co-operative system, the progress of that
system amongst working men will be finished,

If tt I)ont4 "fii to be a bribe for submission, a
bait hel). rimit for profitable exertion on the
part at the operatives of the country, inatead,
as it ought to be, the natural fruit of a higher
and better relationship between capital and
labour, independent, self-respecting working
men will leave it to those who can pocket the
price of their own degradation without trouble
of conscience. Whether the co-operators of
the kingdom approve of this and are prepared
to follow Mr. ARCIIIBILD BRIGGS in this
direction, is a question which I have no doubt
they will answer in their own good time.
This controversy need not be pursued
further. Every true-co-operator will rejoice in
the success attending the efforts of Mr.
Bniaas and his directors, so far as these
efforts square with the true principles and
practices of co-operation. But these men have
no right to saddle a principle with their faults
of temper or defects of policy. They may
hate trades unions, as much as they like, as
coal proprietors, but they must not in the
name of co-operation enter on a war with huge
bodies of skilled, intelligent, and honest men,
who are moving up to the camping ground of
our co-operative army to swell its ranks in
fighting for the emancipation of labour.
Trades unions are the auxiliaries of co-opera-
tion, not its enemies, and though a little
sparring may DOW and then take place between
a few of the half-drilled and ill-tempered on
both sides, no separation of interests or
diversity of principle can bring them into
conflict.
If Mr. BRIGGS and those for whom he acts
would try to perfect the working of their
own scheme, which in the best meaning of the
term is not co-operation, they would soon find
themselves much better and more profitably
empployed than they can be whilst engaged in
exorcising and hunting out the spirit of trades
unionism from amongst working men.
The charge made by Mr. BRIGGS as to the
men leaving their work with any hostile view
on the day of the shareholders' meeting cannot
be correct. The date of the men's meeting at
Leeds, and its object, had been known for a
long time, and small subscriptions entered
into for defraying the expense. Mr. Ramos'
action was sudden and just on the eve of the
meeting.

do we complain that a man so high in posi-
tion as Earl DEBBY should address it to

demanding moderation from the sellers of these

tax his time, and it would, if he published the

value •of land in the thriving town of Bury,

our agricultural labourers will do much to
keep the poor worker contented on this head.

scale, not to "employ more men than the
necessity of the business required" as the

uncalled for. People do not usually employ
more men to do anything than arc necessary
whatever the state of the labour markt,t, awl

' Tun Geneva Arbitrators have decided, it ap-
pears, against England and in favour of
Anierioa. The tax-payers are to be made to
pay a sum of between three and four millions
on account of what I will not call the blunder,
but the gross misconduct of the Government of
Lord PALMERSTON during the Civil War of
America.

The Alabama and other pirate vessels were
built, fitted out, and armed in England, for
the express purpose of attacking the merchant
vessels and destroying the commerce of the
Northern States of America, and all this under
the connivance of the British Government,
which not only sympathised with the Rebel

ber of the same Government, declared on the
same occasion that the North were fighting for
conquest, while the South was fighting for
independance. In short, nearly the whole
aristocracy of England was in favour of
the South, while the whole of the work-
ing classes wished success to the North.

common cause with the Republicans of the

MR. ARCHIBALD BRIGGS AND

I AM glad that Mr. BRIGGS has replied to Mr.
LLOYD JONES' strictures upon the action taken
by the firm of HENRY Bilious and Co., in rela-
tion to the distribution of bonus to members of
trades unions, because it gives those who have
c‘refully watched the action of HENRY
BRIGGS and Co., both before and after their
scheme of industrial partnerships, the oppor-
tunity of placing some of the said actions
before the public in a true light.
There is really no denial of the facts stated
by Mr. JONES in Mr. ARCHIBALD BRIGGS' repllt
but whereas the circular quoted by Mr. JoOs
appeared to threaten the payment of the bonus
actually declared in 1872, Mr. BRIGGS SAYS
now "that no union men shall be entitled to
bonus who pbrsecute their fellow non-unionist
workmen, or seek at any time to stop the
working of our collieries," and "that all who,
in spite of our plain notice, left their work on
the 19th of August, though they have the
bonus for 1872, will not reeeive it for the
current year." Among other things one is
disposed to ask as an instruetive inquiry if the
latter clause is duly provided for in the articles
of their Industrial Partnerships' Association.
If not, how can they now enforce any such
exemption?
The public will also be curious to inquire
why and how it is that Mr. ARCHIBALD
Baroas (for after all it is he who began end
worked the opposition) has such a decided awl
even bitter hatred to union and union men 1'
I have often heard his hits and skits at thew/
open and covert; and though I have never spoken
before of it, I knew well the real cause of his hatred
and objection. The fact is, and the public should
know it, the firm of Messrs. HENRY BRIGGS o'l
Co. were a' mongst the chief causes of tile
existence of the West Yorkshire Miners'Uni'llt
and without the actions which they lad
powerful hand in, in 1858 and. 1861, tiler°
would have been no union at all, and without
'on
this cause, in continuing it, the men's
would long since have died out. Unions ore
not institutions existing on either whims °I:
abstract motives, and had they not suilloialb
causes for operation, they would neither be
worked nor supported at even their trifling

costs in contribution. Before 1858 the West
Yorkshire Miners had no union, but the
master colliers had, and their union met in
March of that year, and issued a notice that on
and after April 3rd. it was their intention to
reduce wages 15 per cent., and that they
should require the usual fourteen days' notice
if the men should leave their employ upon
the new terms. This very modest proposal
made the men bestir themselves at once, and
they resolved not to accept the reduction, and
to form a union to defend themselves from this
unprovoked attack of their masters, - How the
struggle began and ended after a long strike
and then a lock-out; how the men wore
Punished, and starved, and ejected from their
houses and gardens; and how after all the
masters were beaten, and the men maintained
their wages though coal was not advanced;
are they not written in the "Book of Social
Science," vol. iii., and also in the "Book
of the Trades Reports of that Association,
1860," p. 11 to 51? In that struggle of masters
against men Messrs. H. B. and Co. took
an active part. But when the strike was
over, the men, thinking all was over, gave
up their union, and. they had not one
previous to June 12th, 1863, when the Messrs.
Baxaas first gave a notice to reduce wages,
and to introduce riddles into the pit—.
i.e., increase the work. This caused the men
again to unite, and from that time to this
they have maintained the union with various
uperand downs as necessitated. And here
again I affirm that it was the action of the
masters that made the union, and in this
ease the Messrs. BRIGGS took the principal
part in the causing, and the principal action
in the strike and struggle which followed.
The Messrs. Barnes, in order to get riddles
worked. in their pits, induced BOWERS to
introduce riddles also, and that in places
where the men declared. it dangerous for their
lives to 'work them; and because the men
Would not riddle at BOWERS, when Mr. B.
himself admitted it was dangerous, and
where he himself did not wish them to riddle
—the men were by thousands locked-out from
the pits at Methley—prevented getting pit
work in the district, prevented from even
breaking stones on the highway, farm-work,
or any other they could be deprived of. They
Were' 'ejetted from their houses—at those of
the Messrs. Buiaes—with a degree of cruelty
and inhumanity, which the very police (who,
armed with cutlasses, became the involuntary
agents to effect) cried shame upon. For
months, through a very severe winter,
hundreds of families were huddled together
in houses and huts not fit to dwell in, to
the ruin of their health, and scores were
(slaved out in tents upon ground lent to
them, their only mode of living being to beg,
or to perisif and starve, from the tyranny of
Koh as Messrs. Mmes. Blacksheep were
tempted. to come by all sorts of misrepresenta-
tions, by special agents of the Messrs. Bureau
themselves, arid in the end, by the help of In-
spector Ilocx4.nax, of the West Riding police,
the Messrs. BRIGGS gathered togetheit a colliery
of blacks, and tiled the pits with a scum
from Derbyshire, Staffordshire, and wherever
they could. The Messrs. BRIGGS permitted these
to drink in the pits, and allowed them to bully
the men looked out. A teetotaller kept the
barrels of ale to distribute from, and the po-
lice had to keep in the blacks, lest tjxey should
Commit murder in some of their drunken
orgies. Before the, strike, llamas' had a
staff of good and. orderly men, but during
the strike and after, they brought such a set of
roughs that the West Riding magistrates
made a note of it RS not to be tolerated in the
trouble and cost these outlaws made to
the Biding; the result was the Messrs.
BRIGGS, who could not beat the men, did
beat themselves; for with the pits being full
of their own especial men—genuine non-
unionists—the cost of production so increased,
and the work was so difficult to manage, that
they were dead-beaten. They first gave up
the siam
or made good. the prices; they got
back their old men, and to get rid. of the
blacks they proposed bettor terms and better
Working, and, as reported, on a moneyed
partner withdrawing, as a resort, and not
from -
any love of the principle, they professed,
sheerly as a matter of necessity, to become a
'limited liability company, to raise funds, and

set to work an industrial partnership scheme,
to get colliers to work.
Concerning the economic condition of the
firm at the time of the limited liability
and industrial partnership scheme was pro-
posed, the terms of the purchase, and the
wealth of the BRIGGS afterwards, nothing
need be said. Suffice it that, those who
knew the whole stood aloof and said, if
that scheme and. those terms could work,
the wonder of what co-operation could do
would become marvellous, or, that the
profits of coal-working were beyond. credi-
bility, and would prove the fallacy of
the stated necessity for the reduction of
wages which led to the strike. Well, time
went on, the BRIGGS raised money by the
company scheme, and got men to work, less
on their belief upon the bonus idea than upon
better treatment" and working. And. to do
the firm only simple justice, I must state that
$a much superior has been their treatment and
regard to the men generally, that bad any-
thing like that been the case before, there
would have been neither strikes nor indus-
trial partnership.

It was the conduct of the firm which made
all the disturbances before; and it has been
their conduct which has made the peace since.
It was their treatment that made the union,
and force of the union which made them alter
their treatment. And therefore, from first to
last, they hate the union, and blame the union for
successful resistance, instead of blaming them-
selves, for injustice and tyranny. I have heard it
raid that a man, by the exercise of Christian
principle, oan and may forgive another who
has injured him; but that one who tries, and
never forgives the one who escapes, or over-
lives the injury intended. Apply this to the
case of the Messrs. BRIGGS, and we may per-
fectly understand their animus against
unionism. But with what right let the facts
tell; and with what grace the reader may
judge, when it is known that Messrs. BRIGGS
and Co., of the Industrial Partnership Limited,
makes something like 30 per cent. profit upon
capital; that they are members of the Coal
Masters' Union, which fixes the price of coal,
which regulates work and reduces wages, or
restricts -advances; and that they regulate both
their prices of coal and wages by the coal
masters' lists or resolutions. As one result,
incredible as it may be, we may state the
Messrs. BRIGGS and Co. rise the price of their
lists ss. per ton all round; and yet they re-
fused to advance wages more than 3d. per ton
only last week, along with the rest of the coal
masters in union!
There can be no doubt of the fact that the
Messrs. BRIGGS are against the union they did
so much to eause ; and they say that the union
is against them, Well, and what wonder?
But that the union ever has, or even contem-
plates taking action against the well working
of the bonus system, or•even limited liability,
I have never heard. Mr. ARCHIBALD, BRIGG
says, that their non-union workmen are in-
sulted and intimidated; has he ever inquired
if union men are not so treated P If careful
to Shield the one, is he careful to see that the
others are not mblested, and have full justice
done to them? As to the one day taken, and
charged to the union demonstration, as being
against them, why did he not charge the
thirteen preceding Saturdays broken, in
which the union had nothing to do? And why
did the Messrs. Blum put notice in their pits
on Saturday, two or three weeks previous,
that their pits would be closed from
Saturday till the Thursday following, three
working days ! in order to let all the
men have the opportunity of attending the
two days' races at Pontefract ? I am told that
one man of BRIGGS' who worked on the 19th,
went oft' in vexation next day, and drank for
days, until he died of excessive drinking; but,
that the men who attended the demonstration
did not go to work therefore, is to me in-
credible;' seeing that they were especially
advised and requested by their leaders to
do so—unless it was because of the sinister
action of the Arm themselves in unsettling and
disgusting the men in relation to the system of
bonuses. A more orderly gathering so large—
and a more sober return home from such a
demonstration was never even seen or heard
of; and at all other places than at the Bitmos,

the union men went to work, and have con-
tinued to work regularly since. How often
Men make the evils they have to complain
of; and FaANIcENsTEIN. like, the Messrs.
BRIGGS have made the monster which they say
impedes their movements. But that men
should keep up the union for other purposes
than merely to resist tyranny and injustice, I
will treat of in my next, oven though it may
not please Mr. ARCRIBILD Bnraos.

JOHN HOLMES.

articles.title: PRICE OF PP-VISIONS,
articles.text:
THE PRICE OF PP-VISIONS,

On Monday night a meeting, convened by
various democratic and trade societies in
London, and attended by nearly 1,000 persons,
was held in Trafalgar-square, with the aid of
the lime-light, for the purpose of taking steps
to prevent a continuance of the present high
prices of provisions. A procession, mom
panied by a band, arrived from Clerkenwell-
green shortly after eight o'clock. The pro-
moters of the meeting took up a position at
the base of the pedestal of the Nelson Monu-
ment, on the north side, and one of their
number held a red flag, the pole of which was
crowned with the "-cap of liberty," Mr.
Patrick, a mechanical engineer, presided.
Mr. Brighty moved the first resolution,
which was :

That in the opinion of this meeting the present
administration of the Orders in Council, in restrict-
ing the importation of foreign cattle, is not now
used so much to prevent disease as to establish a
system of monopoly and protection in the interests
of the home breeders, which ought not to be
tolerated in a country pledged to free trade.
(Cheers.)
Mr. Magee Pratt seconded the resolution.
The resolution was carried unanimously.
Mr. Wade next moved :-- '

That the present land and game laws are the
principal cause of the high prices of provisions by
restricting the productive power of the land, thus
allowing millions of acres to be devoted to an in-
human sport., and creating an amount of special
crime unknown in any other civilized country;
and this meeting is of opinion that if the land now
appropriated by a small section of society for pur-
poses of selfish pleasure were properly cultivated,
the whole of the population could be well sup-
plied with food at reasonable prices.
The resolution was seconded by Mr. Riddle
and agreed to.
Further resolutions were adopted, urging
upon the Government the expediency of eni-
ploying our surplus labour in the cultivation
of waste lands, and appointing a deputation to
wait upon Mr. Gladstone for the purpose of
inducing him to consider the whole of this
important subject."

articles.title: ;EXIIGRA.TION OF EX-RAILWAY SERVANTS.
articles.text:
THE ;EXIIGRA.TION OF EX-RAILWAY
SERVANTS.

The emigration of
,the dismissed railway
servants of the London and North Western
Cempany—the men who were discharged in
consequence of the strike at Broad-street—is
gradually but steadily progressing. A. second
batch of men has been sent out to Quebec by
the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants,
and a third party of emigrants are preparing
for departure. The society advances £0 to
each man, taking in exchange for the money
the emigrant's note at six mouths' date, so
that the amounts given to assist the men will
turn in again, to be used in a similar or some
other benevolent purpose. Taking into account
the fact that the Amalgamated Society is only
about nine months in existence, its success as
a benefit organization for the railway servants
of the kingdom has been quite unprecedented,
as there are now upwards of 20,000 members
enrolled on its books. How far its financial
operations have been successful is shown by the
fact that in the first week of the strike on the
London and isl orth Western Railway, now some 5
weeks since, a sum of 10s. each was paid to
upwards of 530 men. In the second week 120
men; in the third, 90 men; and in the fourth
week of the strike 80 men received a similar
sum. At the 'present moment more than 70
members of the society are in the receipt of a
weekly sum. The number of men out of em-
ployment has steadily decreased, as.the society
does not confine its assistance to the granting
of money, but gets berths for some, and helps
others to emigrate. Toronto, Upper Canada,
has been up the present the intended destina-
tion of emigrants, and it is understood, from
adviees received from across the ocean, that
those men who are really experienced in rail-
way work will find no difficulty whatever in
obtaining employment on the Canadian lines.
It is proposed to found, in connection with the
society, a Special Emigration Fund.

LONDON.

TRH BUILDERS' LABOURERS.

An open-air meeting of the builders' labourers
of London was held in Trafalgar-square on
Saturday evening to receive the report of their
deputations to the Masters' Association relative to
the late dispute in the trade. It was estimated
that there were fully 1,500 of this class present,
and the proceedings, which occupied about an
hour and a half, were characterized by good
temper' and order from beginning to end. Mr.
Williamson, a labourer, was elected chairman, and
having briefly explained the object of the
gathering, Messrs. Kenny and Halloran, labourers'
representative, on the Amalgamated Building
Trades Committee, gave a report and enforced the
necessity of union, and moved :
That, in the opinion of this meeting, the small
addition granted to the wages of the Builders'
Labourers is not sufficient to enable them to
support themselves and families; and this meeting
of labourers pledges itself tense its influence, and
calls upon all concerned to do the same, to extend
throughout the Londen district the Builders'
Labourers' Union, so that by our united strength
we may be able to command our 6d. per hour.
Mr. J. Leicester seconded the resolution, which,
being passed by acclamation, a vote of thanks was,
on the motion of Mr. Driscoll, seconded by Mr.
Berry, of Kingston on-Thames, "accorded to Mr.
Kenny, the labourers' secretary, for the zeal and
ability with which he advocated the labourers'
claims before the sub-committee of the Master
Builders' Association on Wednesday, the nth of
August last."

BURY.
AGITATION IN TUE IRON:TRADES,

A meeting of operatives emp oyed in the iron
trades at Bury was held on Friday evening. Some
600 operatives were present. The meeting was
convened for the purpose of deciding respecting
a circular, wherein it was:stated that it had been
resolved that a general advance of 2s. per
week should be sought upon the present rate of
wages (about 285,), and that the rate for overtime
be on the following scale :—Time and a quarter for
the first two hours; time and a half for the second
two hours; and double time 'for all time after-
wards on tho same day, each day to stand by
itself; Sunday, Christmas Day, and Good Friday,
or any portion thereof, to be paid double time, to
be calculated on the nine hours' system.
The Secretary said that thirteen firms had been
communicated with, but only three replies received,
viz., from Messrs. Walker and Hacking, Vulcan
Foundry; Robert Hall and Sons, Hope Foundry ;

and Messrs. Cook and Hacking—three of the
leading firms in the town, employing amongst
them nearly 2,000 hands. The effect of these
replies was a refusal to comply with the demands
of the men.

It was resolved that there should be no strike,
but that as soon as practicable fresh situations
should be secured for those won whose employers
will not comply with the demands made upon
them.

THE DYERS.

WOOLWICH. ,
TEE WAGES OP GOVERNMENT WORKMEN.

A meeting of nearly a thousand labourers em-
ployed in the Royal Arsenal Control Department
was held at the Lecture Hall, Woolwich, on Tues-
day evening, to take steps for increasing the
present rate of wages. Mr. M'Culry, a storeholder
in the department, occupied the chair, and said
that owing to tho nine hours movement and
other causes the cost of provisions and other
necesamies of life had risen to such a degree that
the wages which were sufficient to support life
two years ago were quite inadequate now. The
labourers in the Control Department were paid
on entering 16s. a week, which rate continued for
ton years, when the pay was raised to 155., and
after a man had been twenty years in his situation
ho might hope to receive 175., or perhaps 18s. a
week, but no more. Two-thirds of the labourers
were receiving but 155., and there were only 47
in the department who had risen to 18s. lie read
a letter from one of the labourers, a man with a
wife and six children to support on 170. a week,
out of which he had to pay 4s. 6d. for rent, 7s. 6d.
for 'Head, 28. 2d. for light and fuel, 2s. 2d. for tea
and sugar, and 51d. for soap, &e., making 16s. 9ld.
and leaving ( nly 2ld. for meat, clothing, the edu•
cation of his children, and all other purposes. It
was true that in some other departments there
was a Us, rate, but ti.o men there were on piece-
work, and earned 255. or more; but the control
men had no such good fortune.
Mr. Gibson, a coal merchant, and Mr. Baxter
Langley, of London, having addressed the meet-
ing,

Mr. Hemmings, one of the labourers, made a
very energetic speech, in which he said that he
was in comparatively easy circumstances with 17s.
a week and a family of only three, but ho know of
cases in which a man had to keep himself, his wife,
and nine children on 15s. a week. The labourers
of the Royal Arsenal were not hasty in this move-
ment. They were nearly the last section of the
working-classes to appeal for better wages, and
they were but acting upon the counsel of Lord
Derby, who said that every man had a legal and
moral right to promote his own interests. Why,
Mr. Reed, the naval constructor, gave his labourers
255. a week, and even his boys iSs.,which was
more than many men of intelligence, filling re-
sponsible positions in the Arsenal, obtained from
the Government. There was the winter before
them, and unless they had speedy relief they must
starve. The Government could not refuse their
appeal, and they must not delay it until the new
estimates in April. To keep men, women, and
children starving through the hail winter on such
a pittance is cruelty. If there had been a Society
for the Prevention of Cruelty to Mankind as there
was for the brute animals, such a state of things
would have been amended long ago.
Several other labourers addressed the meeting,
and it was resolved to petition the War-office in
favour of an increase of pay to the labourers of the
Control Department, a committee of workmen
being appointed to carry out the necessary arrange-
ments.

GLOSSOP.
TIIE I) PVTI IN TUE COTTON TRADE.

The complications which have arisen in the
Glossop district by the demand of the spinners for
an advance of wages have been 'satisfactorily

A sliort time ago the jobbers employed in the

In the event of an improvement of the trade of

The Operatives' Association expressed them-

articles.title: TRADES UNIONS IN VICTORIA.
articles.text:
TRADES UNIONS IN VICTORIA.

A movement has just been commenced in
Victoria for the purposo of bringing about a union
of trades societies. The importance of the subject
is very great to all manual workers.
It must be obvious to all who pay any atten-
tion to the condition of trades, &c., that manual
workers will suffer severely from the effects of the
groat competition which now prevails in this
colony, unless something is done to counteract
these effects. In connection with this it should
be noted that employers and capitalists ever
demand, and usually obtain, the same profit irre-
spective of the changes of market or of circum-
stances, while the producers have to labour for a
lower remuneration than before. In some trades
this is the case already, and the bitterness of
being underpaid is keenly felt, which is deepened
by the constant attempts of employers to lower
wages still more, while the inability of the
workmen to cope successfully with :capitalists
unaided, is self-evident.

This being seen, it is felt that the time has
come for a grand co-operative union of trades
societies for mutual health and strength. Expe-
rience has shown that single-handed a trade
society (unless very strong) has little chance of
protecting workmen's rights; while on the other
hand the great successes—almost triumphs—of
the union system in England shows what may be
done by combination. In England the results
have been an increase of pay in nearly [every
trade; the gaining of the nine hours system ; and
the recognition of the right of manual workers to
consideration and social elevation.

The following advantages would result from the
formation of a trades association :

18t. Trades would gain strength :—As two are
stronger than one, so that nineteen or twenty
Melbourne trade societies united would be more
powerful than isolated societies.
2nd. Trades would gain the means of enforcing
or retaining their right to "a fair day's pay for a
fair day's work."
3rd. Trades would be in a position to obtain
better treatment and consideration than they now
receive; and, therefore, would not fool the almost
abject dependencq, upon employers which is at
times seen.

4th. By a healthy combination, manual workers
would have greater influence upon social questions
than they now have—they being the majority.
sth. Springing out of the foregoing, manual
workers would obtain a more fair remuneration for
labour—a better socialyposition and a more just
consideration of their worth in the political
economy of the colony. A. union has been formed
upon the broadest foundation ,consh:tent with its
practical working; and, for the present, is based
upon the principles contained in the following
resolution
The United Trades' Association shall be formed
of trade or handicraft societies for the purposes of
mutual assistance, when engaged in obtaining or
retaining rights; the amelioration of the condition
of working men, together with the furtherance of
all objects which may be for the good of manual
workers.

Your earn Est co-operation in the above is then-
fore solicited.

THE COM3IITTEE.

Melbourne, July 13th, 1872.

The Queen visited the Golspie Falls, and

Count Andrassy late on Monday night paid

Chancellor is reported to have used language
importing the entire absence of any desire to
further political schemes in the present meet-
ing of the Emperors, who were engaged in a
mere ceremonial of friendship.

articles.title: LONDON CARPENTERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON CARPENTERS.

On Monday the Carpenters and Joiners' Central
Committee paid their final strike dividend at the
rate of 2s. 6d. a day, or 15s. a week per man.
During the week upwards of 350 signed the strike
sheets; but tint total does not represent the num-
ber actually idle for the whole six days, as by a
resolution of the delegates a man could for the
space of a month come on and off the sheets at
pleasure in the intervals of his being out of work.
The strike began the first week in June with very
nearly the same number as that which shared in
the last dividend. The first dividend paid was at
the rate of 248. a weak per man; the second 275.,
and the third 21s. Then came the "lock-out,"
and with it a fall in the fourth dividend to 7s.
6d.; the fifth was Bs., the sixth Os. (loek-outwith-
drawn), the seventh 10s., the eighth 125., the
ninth, us. ; the tenth, us. 6d. the eleventh, 135.;
the twelfth, 6s. (week after the settlement) ; and
the thirteenth, 15s. The highest, therefore, was
at the rate of 4s. 61. a day, and the lowest Is. a
day.

What has hitherto been called "The Short-time
Movement" will henceforth become a" Uniformity
of Time and Wages Movement ;" and the
business of delegates meetings will be to arrange
for the machinery to extend the adoption of the
agreement recently come ta with the Central
Association of Master Builders to employers out-
side that body. At the last meeting three
prominent firms in this category were brought
under notice, viz., Corbett and McClymont's, West
Brompton ; Adamson and Son's, Turnham-green ;
and Perry and Co.'s, Stratford. These belong to
the nil. class; that is they pay or paid 7id. an
hour only, and -work 56i hours a week. Deputa-
tions from the committee were appointed to deal
with the two first. Messrs. Davis, Benny, and
Matkin (secretary) were delegated to move Corbett
and M4Clymont's, who employ over 50 men, and
they returned with the report that in order to
avert a threatened strike, the firm had uncon-
ditionally accepted the terms of the agreement
entered into with the Masters' Association. The
shop has accordingly commenced working under
the code of rules issued by the Central Committee.
This result is hailed with much satisfaction, as a
very good opening of the now movement to make
the 8111. an hour and 52i hours arrangement as
general as possible throughout the trade. There
is hope that in a very short time newly every
large shop will be brought within the compass of
the recent compact between the masters and men.

articles.title: LONDON CHAIRMAKERS AND CARVERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON CHAIRMAKERS AND
CARVERS.

On Monday night a crowded meeting of chair-
makers and carvers in the cast of London was
held at the Columbia Temperance Hall, Hackney-
road, for the purpose of taking steps to obtain an
advance in their rate of wages.
Mr. Hay, a carver, having been voted to the
chair, stated that they had not instituted the
movement out of any hostility to the masters,
whom they wished to treat with every respect and
fairness. They considered that, seeing the high
prices which prevailed, they were perfectly justified
in endeavouring to get an increase of wages, so as
to enable them to meet and cope with the exigen-
cies and circumstances of the times. He believed
many of the masters—in fact, all the higher class
ones—would at once acknowledge the justice of
their demands, although no doubt the small
masters, by underselling them in the market, were
a great drawback in the way. By, however,
adopting a calm and considerate and reasonable
course, and showing that they wished to accom-
modate their employers as much as possible, he felt
certain they would in the end succeed in their
object.

Mr. Bustall then moved a resolution to the effect
that the meeting was of opinion, looking at the
exorbitant price of every description of provisions,
and the great rise which had taken place irt house
rent, that they were entitled to an increase in their
wages to the extent of at least 10 per cant. He
stated that the firm for which he worked, the
Messrs. Piecard, bad shown every disposition to
meet their men in a fair and honourable manner,
and no doubt others would do the same.
Mr. Wilshire seconded the resolution, which
was adopted unanimously.
It was then resolved to appoint delegates from
each shop to ascertain the -views of the masters
and take steps to carry out the resolution just
adopted.

articles.text:
THE WEST CIIABER.LAND MINERS.

A conference between the coalowners of West
Cumberland and a number of representatives of
the miners of the district was held at Working-
ton on Thursday. Mr. Isaac Pletcher, M.P. for
Cockermouth, presided. The chairman said that
in consequence of the extraordinary demand for
coal prices had gone up and wages had gone UP
.very much. Moreover, a Miners Union had been
established in the district where there had been
none before. He did not find any fault with the
miners for forming such a union. They bad 8
perfect right to do so, for the purpose of bettering
their condition. His own view was that, if there
was a difference, the :workmen should appoint a
man, and the masters should also appoint a Inne'
and let them determine as to what was fair and
right between the parties ; and if the two eoeld
not agree, let them appoint an umpire to decide
between them. The proposal was warmly received
by the representatives of the miners, and the fel-
lowing resolution was unanimously adopted :--
That in case of any dispute between the work-
man at any colliery and their employers, such dispute
shall he settled by arbitration, the mode of carry-
ing out such arbitration to be considered 11 ad
joint committee consisting of three masters an ,
three znen, who will report to an adjournment.ol
this meeting, at a date to be fixed by the char'
man.

articles.title: LONDON BAKER'S.
articles.text:
THE LONDON BAKER'S.

The operative bakers of London, by way of
showing their determination to abide by their
demand for a specified working day of twelve
hours, organized an open-air demonstration in
Lambeth on Saturday evening, and have also held
a second meeting at which the speakers advised
the men to act with firmness and resolution.

They have also issued the following
TO TILE MASTER BAKERS OF LONDON.

_
Gentlemen,—We, the Strike Committee of the
London Trade Council of Bakers, beg most respect-
fully to lay before you the following resolutions
that were carried unanimously at a meeting of
the aforesaid Council, held at the Admiral Carter,
Bartholomew-close' West Smithfield, on the 28th
day of August, 1872
That we do on the 14th day of September, 1872,
give notice to our employers of the following
demands, to come into operation on the 21st day
of September.
1. That we do claim a day's work of 12 hours,
meal time included. _ _ _

2. That we do not begin work before 4 o'clock
in the morning.
3. That we demand to be paid for overtime at
the rate of is. per hour for a foreman, 9d. for a
second hand, and 6d. for a third hand.
4. That we do demand a fixed minimum scale
of wages—namely, forentfm, 30s. per week, and
bread and flour; Scotch fore-hands or sing!e
hands, 265. with bread and flour; second hands,
265., with bread and flour, and third bands, 215.,
with bread and flour.
6. That Sunday bakings shall be abolished.
Seeing the necessity and justness of our re-
quest, we respectfully beg you to take this into
your serious consideration, and the committee
earnestly hope that you will comply with the above,
or otherwise we shall be compelled to cease work
on the above date.

The first levy of h. per man per week for the
support of the strike has just been received by the
committee, and has amounted to a some what
considerable sum. The men, according to the
latest reports, have considerable faith in the
movement. _

On Wednesday afternoon the conference between
the master bakers and the operatives was held at
Anderton's Hotel. There were present eighteen
persons in each interest, that of the employers
being represented by Messrs. Bonthron, Callard,
11'Cash, Clark, Pringle, May, Robertson, Linscott,
Marston, Inglis, Hollis, Maurer, Weston, and
Shelton; and the men being represented by
Messrs. Webb, Hare, Coclaman, Giles, Morison,
Roberts, Baines, Penton, Fairchild, Andreas,
Evershed, How, Adams, Shallis, Strickland, Allen,
Greenwood, and Fink. Mr. E. S. Mantz attended
as Secretary of the Master Bakers' Trade Pro-
tection Society; while Mr. Peter Polo acted in the
same capacity for the London Trades Council of
Operative Bakers. Every member of the men's
delegation was present, but no less than four of the
masters were absent—Messrs. Dwarber, Stevens,
Ayton, and Richardson. It was prJposed that
Mr. Wm. Weston should take the chair, and that
gentleman was chosen, after some discussion, by
ballot.

Mr. ii. Webb (journeyman) opened the business
by moving the adoption of the first principle,

Viz. :-

That a worliing day shall consist of twelve hours,
and not to commence before four o'clock a.m.

Mr. C. Hare (journeyman) seconded the pro-
position.
Some discussion here arose as to how fancy
goods were to be baked in time, and the answer
given was that, where a large fancy business
existed, extra ovens should be erected on the
premiies.

Mr. Ifollis (master) moved us an amend-
inent—
That a working day shall consist of twelve hours,
and not to commence before four in the morning,
and any hour before that to be paid for at the rate
of tuna and a half.
This was seconded by Mr. Bontbron (master).
After a long discussion the amendment of Mr.
Hollis was altered to the following, to meet the
views of Mr. Bonthron and a few others :

That a working day shall consist of twelve
hours, and not to commence before four o'clock,
except in certain shop which shall be known as
night shops, and that the minimum scale of wages
shall be Os. higher than those commencing at four
o'clock.

It was ultimatoly agroed that an adjournment
for sonic days should take place.

After the conference a meeting of the London
Operatives' Council was held, Mr. G. How in the
Chair.
Mr. Peter Pole and the Chairman reported at
some length upon the proceedings, which were
looked upon as generally satisfactory. The ques-
tion was discussed whether the men were now
ready to make a small concession, or to stand out
for a hard and fast line of from four to four. The
arguments of the greater part of the speakers
Were an favour of giving in to the concession
required by the large, full-priced masters. The
question was ultiauttely deferred, for further eon-
eideration.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABOURER S.
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURER S.

WARWICKSUIRL—The National Agricultural
Labourers' Union is beginning to initiate measures
for the systematic emigration of the surplus agri-
cultural population of the country. This inipo r-
tant question was specially considered at the
meeting of the Executive Committee at Leaming-
ton. On Monday the desirableness of emigration
being judiciously carried out was heartily and
unanimously affirmed by the committee as a
means of permanently and effectively improving
the condition of the labouring classes; and the
secretary was directed to ascertain the conditions
on which the various colonial Governments will
assist the agricultural emigrants, so as to giv e
labourers desirous of emigrating the widest pos-
sible choice. It was announced that the agent of
the Queensland Government had had an interview
with the secretary on the subject, and had con-
sented to waive certain conditions so that addi-
tional advantages would be enjoyed by emigrants
connected with the Union. It is also expected
that special facilities will be offered in other
quarters. The Union has previously assisted
emigrants; but this is the first time it has taken
the initiatory. It was stated that funds will be
forthcoming to provide numbers of labourers with
free passages.

OxronnsurnE.—The three members for Oxford-
shire spoke at the Bicester agricultural dinner on
Thursday, in accordance with their usual custom.
Colonel North, in returning thanks for "The
Army, Navy, and Auxiliary Forces," remarked
that the greatest credit was duo to Mr. Cardwell
for having initiated the Autumn Manceuvres now
going on. The country at large was at last
opening its eyes to the fact that the British
soldier was a man to bo appreciated, and nothing
had tended more to bring about this feeling than
the Autumn Manomvres. Ho continued—" We
cannot allow the bounties of heaven to be de-
stroyed merely because of a difference between
employers and employed." There was no doubt
that the agricultural labourers had been hum-
bugged and deluded by a set of men who did not
care two straws for their interest, and whose only
object was to look out for themselves. The speaker
intensified Bishop Ellicott's figure of speech, and
remarked that the best position for those who
gave the working men " pernicious advice "
would be "a ducking or drowning in the nearest
village pond."
STAFFORDBILIREI.—Lord Lyttelton, in a letter to
the Spectator, says he does not know what he has
been reported to have said about the agricultural
labourers at Stourbridge, but this is what he meant
to say :—" 1. That I thought the labourers not
the least to blame in combining in any way they
pleased. 2. That I thought they must themselves
regret the necessity, if it be so, of being guided
by those mho had only a theoretical know:edge of
the subject, but that in their circumstances it was
almost inevitable for them to be led by some one
or other ab extra. Thirdly and mainly, that I hoped
they and their advisers would accurately consider
the precise object at which they aim. On this
I wish to speak a little more deliberately. I
mean to inculcate generally the substance of some
able letters by Mr. Greg in the Pall Mall Gazette
a few weeks ago.
Is it the object of the labourers' friends that he
should have in money the full market value of his
work? Labourers now, like other people who
have something to sell, get one year with
another about what it is worth, for no one can
get much mon) or much less for any length of
thne. But they got it partly in money and partly
in kind, the latter, no doubt, indicating the
straggling relics of ancient feudal manners, and
consisting of a great variety of subventions which
were ably outlined by Mr. Grog, but which it is
hardly necessary to specify to readers of tolerable
information. This is one groat distinction between
agricultural and manufacturing labour. And it
is perfectly certain that if the two are to be assi-
milated, and Mr. Carlyle's "cash-nexus " is to
rule supremo in both, it will be done completely.
The labourer will get his full money-wages, and
'he will get nothing else at all. I much doubt
whether this is what they mean. Wages, speak-
ing roughly and taking a given sum for conve-
nience, are to he raised from 12s. to 15s. The
probability is that the 3s. more than represents
the additions in kind which the labourer used to
receive from his emp!oyers and those above him.
They will all go, and he will have the money pure
and simple. My belief is that he looks, speaking
of labourers generally, for both—the full money
value and the traditional additions besides. But
this is impossible. I said that he gets now about
what he is worth. It is probable that he, in fact,
gets a little more, when it is rigidly estimated. I
remember the first Lord Ashburton saying in the
house of Lords that probably hardly any farmer
gave barely what he could not help giving to his
men. Lord Radnor' a stiff old economist, replied
at once : " Yes ; but wages are the price of labour,
and whatever the farmer gives more is not wage,
but gift." So it is, properly speaking ; and it is
certain that that state of things must and ought to
be swept away?

In conclusion Lord Lyttolton says :—" We are
threatened with a winter a strikes, and leck-euts,

starvation and rick-burning. The reference is to
the disastrous times of 1830 an! thereabouts.
Now what was the measure which, according to
the general and I believe the correct opinion, did
more than any other direct agency to ameliorate
that state of things? The answer is instructive ;
a new and stringent poor-law."
NEWARK.—A great demonstration is to be held
hero next Tuesday, at which several leading repre-
sentatives of working men are to be present.
WISBEACIL—A demonstration will be held here
on Wednesday, and a tea meeting; both are to
be on a grand scale.

articles.title: LONDON AMALGAMATION OF CABINET MAKERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON AMALGAMATION OF
CABINET MAKERS.

On Saturday afternom, at 5 o'clock, 140
cabinet makers, independent of friends and mem-
bers of their families, sat down to tea in the hall
of the People's Gardens, Willesden, to celebrate
the amalgamation of the Alliance Cabinet Makers'
Association and the East London Cabinet Makers'
Society.
After tea there was 'promenade and dancing on
the monstre platform in front of tha hall, while
the scene was enlivened by the excellent band
belonging to the Gardens. The weather was pro-
pitious, and it would be difficult to select an
evening more suitable for a picnic party. As if
envy had taken wings and fled, all seemed
resolved to enjoy themselves.
At a meeting held in the hall at 7.30, Mr.
Itarry Ham occupied the chair.
The chairman said they wore fully aware of
the object of this meeting, and he hoped for suc-
cess to the united societies. There were men in
our own trade who would laugh at our exertions,
but it is by union, and by union alone, that we
can obtain success. Since the amalgamation of
the London Cabinet Makers' Societies we have
doubled our funds, and increased 013 number of
our members. He considered this meeting a great
suocess.

Mr. Langridge said he had been loyal to the
best of his ability to the East London Cabinet-
makers' Society, and he now intended to be loyal to
the Amalgamated Society. He was no orator, for
as soon as he became an orator he ceased to be a
cabinet maker. He hoped the day was not far
distant when every difficulty should be removed,
and when the association should extend beyond
London.

Mr. Breese expressed himself in favour of the
amalgamation.

Mr. Bright said he thought they should not
discuss the differences between the East End and
West End Societies, but go on with the presenta-
tion.

The Chairman said when Mr. Smith became
secretary, the East End Society was in a critical
position. lie thought success in a great measure
depended on him. The society had voted Mr.
Smith .£lO, part of which had been expended in
purchasing a handsome timepiece, enclosed in a
glass shade, which he had much pleasure in pre-
senting him. He thought he fully deserved it.
Mr. Smith, who was much cheered, said he
thought they made a mistake, as one could do
nothing unless supported by ell. lie thought
trades unions wera beneficial, as the members
could ask assistance as a right, not as a f tvour.
He sincerely thanked them, and would appreciate
their mark of approval as long as he lived. No
one had found fault with him, and again thanking
them, be hoped they would be united for many
years to come.
Mr. Ham (chairman) was warmly congratulated,
and after a cordial vote of thanks for his services,
the proceedings wera closed.

articles.title: RAILWAY SERVANTS.
articles.text:
THE RAILWAY SERVANTS.

LONDON AND SOUTII WESTERN CLERKS.

The clerks engaged in the goods department at
Nine Elms recently presented to the directors a
memorial, embracing as signatories the entire

staff, praying for an increase in salary, to meet
the enhanced cost of living consequent upon the
advanced price of all necessary household com-
modities. And as the company, conjointly with
other leading lines, have lately raised their goods
tariff, it was confidently hoped the boon craved
would be acceded to, more especially that its
motive principle was similar with that which
induced the company to advance their rates, viz.,
the necessity to meet an extra expenditure, the
men orialists being in addition a class of men
never at any time over-paid. The answer received
was, however, universally considered unsatis-
factory, inasmuch that only 30 out of tho 140
old signatories participated in the advance made.
Tho selections were also deemed illogical and
invidious, so that during the past week indig-
nation meetings have been wiled to consider what

steps should be taken to obtlin more general
recognitions, at which it was decided a committee
representing one clerk from each department
should wait upon the goods manager, Mr. J. S.
liaddow, and call his attention to the pervading
disaffection, and the causes giving rise to it. The
deputation was most courteously received, and a
promise given that a revised list shall be framed
for submission to the general manager, and
through him to the directorate, with a view of
dealing more impartially with the main body of
the clerks.

articles.title: MANCHESTER RAILWAY PORTERS.
articles.text:
MANCHESTER RAILWAY PORTERS.

A numerously-attended meeting of the railway
porters in the Manchester district was held on
Sunday, at the Free-trade Hall, to consider the
question of wages and the hours of work. Up to
lately the wages of the railway porters in this
district have been 20s. per week, but recently
some have received an advance of Is. per week.
It being thought that the entire body are entitled

increasing according to length of service, which

appear to be satisfactory to the majority of those

all. Another resolution was passed to the effect

namely, 10 hours per day for the first five days
and seven and a half hours for Saturday; and
that any man not working that tune should still
be allowed for a full week, provided ho had been
on duty all the hours that the Company requ:red.
It was also resolved to request the railway boards
to allow a three-day holiday each year, with
wages paid, and free passes for the mon and
their wives on any part of the respective corn-
p tnies' lines under whom they were employed.

OPENING OF THE BETHNAL-GREEN
MUSEUM ON SUNDAYS.

A public meeting was held in Shoreditch
Town Hall on Wednesday night, and was
attended by several hundreds of the surround-
ing population, to consider the propriety of
opening the Bethnal-green Museum on Sunday
afternoons. The chair was taken at eight
o'clock by Sheriff Sir John Bennett, with
whom there were on the platform the Rev.
R. M. M'Laughlan, Dr. Baxter Langley, Dr.
Bowkett, Rev. Charles Voysey, Mr. G. Eteary,
Mr. J. K. Applobee, Mr. Bradlaugh, and
others.
Sir John Bennett said that in the midst of a
population of 600,000 souls, there had sprung
up amongst them at that most neglected end
of London a building of great magnificence
and beauty. A man of stupendous fortune,
who had collected a magnificent display of
paintings, determined to lend them for the
enjoyment of the people of Bethnal green.
(Hear, hear.) Well, many men were so deeply
immersed in pursuits of industry that there
Was only one 'lay in the week on which they
could find time to see the great display which
had been placed at their service. (Hisses,
followed by great cheering.) Was it the wish
of those who supplied the building that
it should not be opened on Sundays? (Yes.)
He would challenge that assertion. If
they wont to the Government there was a
majority in favour of the opening. Was it
against the will of the man who supplied the
pictures? That man said he desired above all
things that the museum should be open at
times, and especially on Sundays, when the
collection was most likely to be of service to
them. (Hear, hear.) He denied that it would
be injurious to the morality of the people. On
the contrary, visits to the museum would tend
to promote that refinement in art and taste
which was now found among working men on
the Continent to a greater extent than in
England. As for the Sunday question, that
must be solved shortly, or it will solve itself.
(Cheers.)
I letter was read from the Bev. Septimus
Hansard, rector of Bethnal-green, _ in which he
said that nothing but good would result from
the exhibition of Sir Richard Wallace's
pictures on Sunday afternoons. Letters were
read from the Rev. J. Rodwell, and Mr. Currie,
of the London School Board, in favour of the
opening.
Mr. Thomas Reid moved the following re-
solution :

That, recognising that Sunday is wisely set apart
for the purposes of rest, worship, and recreation by
the mass of the people, and seeing that public
museums and art. galleries provide rational and
elevating recreation, which are proved to have had
the most beneficial results wherever the Sunday
opening experiment has been tried, this meeting
calls upon the Government to extend the principle
to the l3ethnal-green Museum,

Dr. Bowkett seconded.
The Rev. Mr. Pieton contended at great
length that neither literally nor in the spirit
could it be shown that under the Christian dis-
pensation people were to be prevented from
making such 'use of the Sabbath as they
thought best. (Hear, hear.) The present
position of the Sunday question was a system
of intolerable and unblushing national hypo-
crisy.
The Rev. C. Voysey, who was greeted with
loud cheers, said that this was the first time
he had stood on a public platform to make a
speech, but he had stifled his prejudices in
order to come there to support the movement
for the opening of Bethnal-green Museum on
Sunday—as a minister of religion. (Cheers.)
Mr. Turner advanced to move an amend-
ment. Did that borough, or any other large
pfoportion of it, demand the opening of the
museums on Sundays? (" Yes, yes," and
"No," the affirmatives predominating.) There
were 360,000 inhabitants in Hackney, and he
protested against any reply of the meeting
being held as the reply of the majority of the
people. As far as his information and in-
quiries went, at least six to one of the inha-
bitants of the borough were prepared to vote
in the negative to the proposal. Then, he
asked, was the opening of the museum floss-
sary now ? (" Yes, yes," and "No.") The
museum was open on Monday, Tuesday, and
Saturday nights until ten o'clock.
The speaker was here interrupted by deter-
mined and noisy opposition, which continued
for several minutes, and he resumed his seat.
Mr. Webber attempted a speech in seconding
the motion, but coAld not succeed.
The Rev. Joseph Bardsley, rector of Spital-
fields, submitted that if the superiority of
Continental workmen in matters of taste was
due to the opening of the museums on Sun-
days, the superiority of Englishmen in other
respects might be fairly attributed to our
national observances. if those who supported
the opening of museums on Sundays would
not Shear arguments on the other side, the
public woulkt naturally infer that they had
come to a foregone conclusion.
After Dr. Baxter Langley sand Mr. Brad-
laugh had, both failed in obtaining a hearing,

That serious evils being found to result from

GRAMME.

On Thursday evening Mr. George Howell,
of London, lectured in the Mechanics' Institute,
Bradford, on the "Working Men's Political
Programme." Mr. James Wallwork pre-
sided, and briefly introduced the lecturer. In
the course of his remarks Mr. Howell said that
he thought they ought to go a little further
than they had hitherto gone with regard to
the extension of the franchise. Not only would
he consider the Reform Bill of 1867 incomplete
till household suffrage had been extended to
the counties, but till every man who had
arrived at years of maturity had a vote. He
stated that there were sixty-five places with
a register of voters of from 1,000 down to
134 (referring to Portarlington) sending to
Parliament seventy members, while the popu-
lation of the places so represented was only
equal to about that of Manchester, which had
only three members. He compared the re-
presentation of constituencies in respect of the
amount of the imperial taxation paid, and
pointed out the inequalities which existed
on this score. There were, he said, thirty
small places, with half the number of electors
of Bradford, with a population not much
larger, and ming less imperial taxation,
which sent thirty members to Parliament,
while Bradford only sent two. He then
referred to the several plans which had been
propounded for remedying the evils of which
the great commercial centres complained in
this respect, favouring particularly the system
of preferential voting ,as proposed by Mr.
Walter Morrison, M.P. On the question of
land tenure reform, he discarded the theory of
the nationalisation of the land as a fitful dream
of the future—an abstract question which
might be discussed by political economists—
and advocated the adoption of such amend-
ments of the law of primogeniture and entail
as would benefit the people directly. He
urged that the land should be free; that they
should be able as expeditiously to convey it as
they did a bale of goods; that it should pay
its full share of the taxation; that the
15,000,000 of acres of waste land in the count
_

try capable of cultivation should be brough;
into cultivation for the benefit of the State
and that all common lands should be
preserved for the benefit of future genera-
tions, no lords of the manor or proprietors
being allowed to convert them into private
property. In regard to taxation, he oonsi-
dbred that we were not so much overtaxed as
wrongly taxed, and went on to show that the
wealthy classes, with incomes of £l,OOO and
over, paid only £8,500,000, whereas they
ought to pay, if charged on the value of their
property, £23,437,688. The working-class on
salaries of a £lOO, paid 32,861,474, and
thus paid five times more than their wealthy
neighbours or, putting it in another way, the
wealthy paid at the rate of 10d. in the pound
i —the working men at the rate of 4s. 4d. n the
pound. The speaker further referred to the
question of trades unions and their action in
relation to capital and labour; and in the
course of his remarks, stated that a rise of 15
per cent, to the collier upon his wages meant
a difference in the cost of getting the coal to
the pit bank of from 30. to 41d. per ton. He
conoludel by referring to the Truck Bill, the
Criminal Law Amendment Act, and the Mines
Regulation Act, and the direct representation
of labour in Parliament. The proceedings
terminated with the usual votes of thanks.
