articles.text:
THE IRONFOUNDERS' SOCIETY
AND INTERNATIONALISM.

We quote the following from this month's
report of the Society which Mr. D. Guile so ably
conducts : •

We shall with this Monthly give you :the
Contents of a letter received from the President of
American Iron Moulders' Union, as well as for-
ward you a voting paper on tho various proposi.
tions laid down as useful to form the nucleus of a
good understanding between the two associations,
merely premising that the sentiments contained in
the letter, as well as the principles laid down in
the propositions, with a little emendation, has the
hearty concurrence of your executive committee
and general officers. The propositions are as
follows :

" First.—That members of the Friendly Society
of Ironfounders of England, &c., will not enter
into any written contracts to work in any foundry
in the United States or Canada, the workmen of
which may be on strike, or locked-out, or in
dispute with their employers previous to their
arrival in either country.

"Second.—That the Iron Moulders' Interna-
tional Union will designate in each seaport city
or town in which they have a juriidiotion, a
member of its union to whom all members of the
friendly society can upon their arrival apply to
for information and advice; and that every mem-
ber of tho friendly society may know at all
times where and to whom to apply.
"Third.—That the executive departments of
the two societies maintain a regular monthly cor-
respondence, and that portions or the whole
thereof be published in their respective journals
or reports.

"Fourth.—Every member of the friendly so-
ciety who shall deposit his card from the fliendly
society, in any of our branches within one month
after his arrivhl, and within one Week after he
secures employment under the jurisdiction of a
local union, shall be admitted to all the privileges
and benefit of our organization without the pay-
ment of any entrance or initiation fee, simply by
taking the obligation provided for new members.
The names of every member of the friendly
society so admitted to be sent regularly to the
executive department of the friendly society.
"Fifth.—Any member of the friendly, society
who shall fail to deposit his card within boo week
after he shall have secured employment under a
local union of the Iron Moulders' International
Union, provided he has been requested to do so,
his name shall be forwarded to the executive de-
partment of the friendly society, and should such
member rettira to the jurisdiction of the friendly
society, he shall be dealt with according to the
decision of the executive committee."

articles.title: DISESTABLISHMZNT.
articles.text:
DISESTABLISHMZNT.

PLAN OF NEXT CAMPAIGN.

The Committee of the Liberation Society have
issued the following plan for their next year's
operations :

To an aggressive party it 18 of great importance
to have a distinct conception of the object aimed
at, and to be thoroughly
•united in regard to the
means by which it is to be pursued. And in both
those respects the advocates of Disestablisliment
will begin the new campaign under very favour-
able circumstances.

This time a year ago it had not been determined
whether the question should be again brought be-
fore the House of Commons, by means of a motion,
in the session of 1872, and, when that course was
subsequently agreed upon, there was, it must be
admitted, some disagreement as to the kind of
motion which would be expedient, as well as some
uncertainty whether it would be possible to sub-
mit the motion ultimately agreed upon.
Circumstances which we need not explain led
the liberation leaders to determine, even before
the close of the recent session, that it would be
wise on the part of Mr. Miall to bring forward
another motion next session; to do it sufficiently
early in the session to ensure a thorough discus-
sion; to put the motion in such a shape as would
raise the question at issue in the most direct and
the boldest terms; and, by giving it early pub-
licity, to make it the basis of operations during
the months of autumn and winter.

In pursuance of this plan, Mr. Miall, shortly
bofore the prorogation, gave notice that early next
session he would move :

That, in the opinion of this House, the estab-
lishment by law of the Churches of England and
Scotland involves a violation of religious equality ;
deprives those Churches of the right of self-
government ; imposes on Parliament duties which
it is incompetent to discluage, and is hurtful to
the religious and political interests of the com-
munity, and, therefore, ought no longer to be
maintained.

Stn. A, 1872.,

Nobody will deny that this is as decisive ne
straightforward, and as explicit as such a motion
can he. It also pats the case against the existing
system suggestively.and comprehensively, as well
as enunciates propositions which the upholders of
that system will find it very difficult to controveit.
For these reasons it has, we believe, been received
with great satisfaction by those whose principles
it is designed to advance, and even opponents
admit that it 18 not open to some of the objections
urged against the motion of July last.
The next step to be taken is to provide that tbifi
motion shall be made the specific subject of Ole
agitation to be carried on during the approaching
season; that its several positions shall be the
texts of lecture, speech, and tract; and that those
who resist the motion shall be distinctly challenged
to disprove their truth. This will give directness
and point, and, to a certain extent, freshness to the
arguments and appeals of anti-state-churchmen,
and will also compel " Church Defenders" to ex-
change something like close reasoning for irrelevant
generalities.

The time has also come when new practical
measures should be adopted to afford to Mr. Mittll
the support which he is entitled to receive. Hitherto
only public meetings and resolutions, the opinions
of a section of the public press, and private color
munications with members, have testified to the
strong approval with which his motions have been
regarded by a large section of the community.
These have, necessarily, been confined to those
places in which such action is practicable, and
have afforded very inadequate evidence of the
earnestness and the resoluteness of puepose of
which Mr. Miall's motions have been the expres.
sion.

Petitioning has, as we are aware, fallen into some
disrepute, because of the multitude of petitions
now annually presented to Parliament, and of the
improper means sometimes employed to obtain
them. But petitions in support of the motion to
be moved next session will be likely to prove ad.
vantageous in several respects. If numerous, an&
largely signed, they will dispel the notion enter.
tamed by some politicians that Mr. Miall's
followers are noisy, but few. They will also aerie
as a means of educating the community more
generally available than meetings and lectures, and
more practical than mere tract-distributing. They
will help us to carryon the warfare in places
where no other weapon can be used; will elicit the
opinions of particular religious bodies hitherto
believed to be in sympathy, but not very actively
co-operating with us; and will give employment
to many willing hands hitherto idle for want of
specific work.

For these reasons, we hope that the call for
petitions will be responded to readily and univer..
sally; so that there will be no reason to regret
that it was determined on, and that Mr. Miall;
when he rises in his place in the spring of next
year, may feel that the House of Commons, how-
ever it may dispose of his motion, will be unable
to despise those whose viewsit represents.
Next month we shall enter into details rela-
ting to the forthcoming movement, which we have
now described in general terms; and, therefore;
we only add; as the last point in our programmet
that the new campaign is to be commenced at an
unusually early period. It will open with a
Midland Counties Conference and a great public
meeting at Birmingham, on Tuesday, the Ist of
October; and the fact that the Nonconformist
Committee of the town have resolved to make
both gatherings as successful as possible, suffi-
ciently guarantees that the work of another
season will be begun effectively as well as early.
The four months which will elapse before the
next season begins will, if wisely used, an ;sae foe
a movement which will very appreciably advance
our cause. And, in addition to all the arguments
and illustrations which our own skill and obser-
vation may suggest, the events occurring every
week in the Established Church will afford us
help of inestimable value; for all the activity of
the Church Defenee Institution does nothing to
abate the scandals and the divisions prevailing
within that Church. Thus, while the assault
continues steadily from without, the process Of
disintegration goes on surely, and more and more
apparently, within. Time, which does not ex"
haust our patience, undermines the Established
system, and perseverance, combined with
practical
wisdom, will inevitably ensure its downfall.

SEPT. 14, 1872.

SOCIAL SCIENCE CONGRESS.

At Plymouth the sixteenth annual Congress of
the National Association for the Promotion of
Social Science commenced its operations on Wed-
nesday, under the presidency of Lord Napier
and Ettrick, K.T. The Council held a meeting at
the Plymouth Institute at 1 o'clock, and at 3 the
members aud associates attended a special service
In St. Andrew's Church. The Mayors and Cor-
porations of Plymouth and Dovonport wore also
present. The sermon was preached by the Rev.
Brooke Lambert, vicar of Tamworth.
A large and influential assemblage was col-
lected in St.
.James's-hall at night to hear the
President's Inaugural Address. Lord Napier and
Ettriek appeared on the platform accompanied by
Earl Fortescue, Sir S. Northoote, M.P., Sir J.
Bowring, Mr. E. Bates, M.P., Mr. R. N. Fow-
ler, M.P., Mr. Kennaway, M.P., the Mayors
of Plymouth, Davenport, and Bodrain, Mr. G.
W. Hastings, Mr. T. Hare, &c. The Pre-
sident's Address, which occupied more than
an hour and a half in its delivery,
Was listened to with unbroken interest
and attentimi, especially when Lord Napier and
Ettrick gave the results of 111;s personal observa-
tion and experience in regard to the emancipation
of the Russian serfs, and the telf-respect induced
among the natives of, India by their personal in-
terest in the soil. His suggestive examination of
the laws regulating the tenure of land, especially
the law of primogeniture and entail, based in
some degree upon his own experience in the South
of Scotland, and his recommendation to landlords
to provide freehold rates for labourers' cottages,
elicited many subdued cries of " Hear, hear."
'When the President resumed his seat the applause
was loud and long continued.
Sir Stafford Northcote said that, in the absence
bf Sir John Pakington, the' last President of the
Congress, it became his duty to move a vote of
thanks to Lord Napier and Ettrick for his instruc-
tive and eloquent address.
Lord Fottescue, in seconding the motion, said
that the intellectual pleasure with which he had
listened to the address had been much enhanced
by the recollection of the old college friendship
which had existed between himself and the Presi-
dent.

The motion having been put by the Mayor of
Plymouth (Mr. Latimer) and carried by acclama-
tion, Lord Napier and Ettrick acknowledged the
compliment in a few well-chosen words, and tho
proceedings terminated.
The several departments met on Thursday in
the rooms allotted to them as follows :—Jurispru-
dence and Amendment of the Law—President, Sir
John D. Coleridge, M.P., Attorney-General ; Re-
pression of Crime Section—President, Mr. J. H.
Kennaway, M.P., Royal Hotel; Education—Mr.
G. W. Hastings, Royal Hotel; Health—Presi-
dent, Dr. Acland, F.R.S., Mechanics' Institute;
Economy and Trade—President, Sir John Bow-
ring, LL.D., Guildhall. The event of the day
was the delivery of the Attorney-General's
address on Jurisprudence and Amendment of the
Law. .In the evening the Mayor of Plymouth
gave a reception at the Assembly Rooms.

articles.title: GOVERNMENT AND THIRD-
articles.text:
THE GOVERNMENT AND THIRD-

CLASS PASSENGERS.

pent the _Railway News.)

The experiment which was recently made by
the northern railways of allowing third-class
Passengers to travel by all trains has not been
one from which the companies have at present
derived any great pecuniary advantage. On its
first adoption considerable loss was, as might
haVo been expected, sustained, but the change is
one the merits of which cannot be adequately
tested in the short period during Which it has been
in operation. It appears quite clear that the
Change has been a direct boon to the second-class
Passengers, who have largely availed themselves
of the opportunity of travelling at lower rates in
third-class carriages. It is not so clear, however,
whether the additional facilities given have
caused so large an increase in the number of those
who have availed themselves of the opportunity
of travelling third-class as is supposed in some
quarters. There has been no doubt during the
last six months a very large increase of thirdhlass
passengers. Tested by the receipts from passen-
gers carried, the increase in the thirtetn weeks in
which the change has been in operation has been
below the standard, which we might have expected
Lad the old system remained in operation.. Thus,
In the thirteen weeks ending June 30, as compared
'with the corresponding period of last year, the
increase on the Great Western was but per
cent., on the Midland 11, on the Great
Northern 4, on the Lancashire. and York-
shire 5, and on the London and North-Western

51. The average increase was consider ably
below that which would have
.occurred to the
railway companies, assuming that the same rate of
increase had been maintained as in the previous
period of thirteen weeks. In the ease of three of
these railways, the reports of which have been
published—viz., Midland, London and North-
Western, and Great Northern—we find that the
total increase in the number of third-class passen-
gers carried was 6,290,000, but there was a falling
off of 1,299,000 of second-class passengers. Of the
4,000,000 remaining after deducting the second-
class passengers
.we Jmight have expected, judging
from the rates of increase of the previous half-
year, to have had at least 2,500,000, so that the
increase in the number of passengers, due to the
permission to travel by all trains, is about
1,600,000, while, as we have shown, the increased
receipts have been much lass than they would
have been under the old system, working expenses
at the same time showing a very considerable in-
crease. We think, then, that it is at present too
early to congratulate shareholders on the results
of the change, though we have no doubt that
ultimately the change will involve no serious loss
to the companies adopting it, and that it may
eventually lead to the disuse altogether of the pre-
sent second-class arrangement, leaving only two
classes of passengers to be accommodated in the
trains, the middle•class either ascending to the
first or descending to the third. This will prove
a much More simple arrangement than the pre-
sent division, it being of course understood that
the companies cannot then—as they do not now—
profess to be responsible for the morals or manners
of those they undertake to convey in their car-
riages at so much per mile.

This increased facility for railway travelling,
conceded to the public, without any demand for it,
but. simply resulting from the action of that
competition the existence of which some people
profess to deny, has served to illustrate in -a
striking manner the mode in which tho Govern-
ment, if left to manage these matters, would treat
the public. It has been intimated to the railway
comp'anies that the Inland Revenue officers will
insist upon thq payment of the Government duty
on third-class passengers, from which the com-
panies have hitherto been exempt, unless the
trains conveying this class of passengers stop at
all the stations. We hope, when next we hear
of the great advantages which the public are to
derive from the absorption of railways by the State,
that this attempt on the part of Government to
nullify the benefits of railway competition will not
be lost sight of by the advocates of Government
purchase of railways. The attempt on the part of
the Government to discourage speed in railway
travelling by the imposition of duty upon all
passenger trains that do not stop at every station
is one of the most remarkable of the many Curious
illustrations afforded of the mischievous inter-
ference of the State in matters with which it has
no concern. As Mr. Moon very truly stated at the
London and North-Western meeting, it is high
time that the position of railways with respect to
State action and control wero settled upon some
reasonable and sensible basis.

"Either," he said, "the Government must take
the railways, or they must make some change
from the present divided personal responsibility
of the Board of Trade and the companies. The
Board of Trade had power to interfere in almost
all the details of management. At present the
Board of Trade was fully as respowible as the
directors, or more so, for accidents which occurred
on the line. The company were liable for the
acts of its [servants, but the Board of Trade
approved all signals and changes on the line, and
they also approved all bye•laws, and therefore
there was little else to do. The managers of the
railways were at issue with the Board of Trade on
many serious points of traffic management con-
nected both with responsibility and safety, and
therefore he repeated that the Government must
either take the railways or invent some other
machinery in place of the present divided responsi-
bility."

Why ought a fisherman to be well ofr ?
Because all he gets is net profit.
Why is IT the gayest letter in the alplial)3l, ?
Because it is always in fun.
The people of Bake Mills, Michigan, dissatisfied
with the name of their town, have changed it to
the hardly more euphonious name of Gobleville.
It is hard to say just now (says an American

quitoes, the politicians, or the dog days.

looking at a lake by moonlight, "see how the
moon sprinkles down on the water ! "

are coming into vogue among the churches, as a
sort of supplement to strawberry festivals
The value of landed estates registered at the

Several lame beggars were completely cured by
the last earthquake which shook San Francisco.
They were able to make as good paces as the
nimblest people in the streets.

difficulties in the pronunciation of the English

lady aged eighty, who recently married a man
of corresponding appropriate age, because, she
said, "he ccmes about my house so much that if

The statistician of an American newspaper avers
that the flies are so good-natured this season that a
well-organised one will allow himself to be
brushed off one's nose eighty-seven times and not
show any temper.
There is a man employed as a porter on a rail-
way who brags of having a watch that keeps
correct time. He was heard to remark, not many
mornings since, upon pulling out his watch," If
the sun ain't over that hill in a minute and a-half,
he will be late."

Young writers will do well to remember that
Lord Bacon re-wrote one of his works twelve
times; and Pascal his letters several times, and
one of them thirteen limes; while Edmund
Burke had his works printed two or three times
on A private press before offering them to a pub-
lisher. •
A traveller relates that while he was in Utah
Tom Thumb was also there on a visit. While
the renowned dwarf was at a dinner party, he
jumped from his chair and said, with a pompous
air, "I cannot understand this polygamy at all."
His host, a man six feet high, thereupon ex-
claimed, "Neither could I, Tom, when I was your
size."

A good story is told of Thomas Carlyle. It is
said that a lady near him kept Cochin China
fowls, and the crowing was such a nuisance that
the philosopher sent in to complain of it. The
lady appealed to was indignant. "Why," she
said, "the fowls only crow four times a-day, and
how can Mr. Carlyle be seriously annoyed at
that?" "The lady forgets," was the character-
istic rejoinder," the pain I suffer in waiting for
those four crows."

A thick-headed squire, being worsted by Sydney
Smith in an argument, took his revenge by ex-
claiming, "If I had a son who was an idiot, by
Jove, I'd make him a parson!" "Very probably,"
replied Sydney; "but I see your father was of a
different mind!"

Brougham one day, speaking., of the salary to be
attached ta a rumoured appointment of a new
judgeship, said it was "all moonshine." Lynd-
hurst, in his dry and waggish way, remarked,
"May be so, Harry; but I've a confounded strong
notion that, moonshine though it be, you would
like to see the first quarter of it."
A celebrated wit was asked why he did not
marry a young laiy to whom he was much
attached. "I know not," he replied, "except the
great regard we have for each other."

An Irishmati, Who liv€4l in an attic, being asked
what part of the house he occupied, answered,
"If the house were turned topsy-turvy, I'd be
liviu.' on the first."

comparing the countenance of a monkey to that
of one of his f How members of Parliament.
Turning, he saw the gentleman had overheard his
remarks, so to make matters pleasant he said, "I
do not knoN which to apol)B,ise t, you or the
monkey."

A man in a. passion spoko many scurrilous
won's; a friend being by, said, "You speak
foolishly." "lie answered, "It is that you may
understand me."

The following grim words handle a ghastly
subject :—" A conclusive argument against sui-
cide is that it is the height of impoliteness to go
anywhere till you are sent for."

A good natured traveller fell asleep in a train,
and was carried a few miles beyond his destina-
tion. "Pretty good joke this, isn't it P" said he
to a fellow passenger. "Yes, but a little too fur
fetched," was the rejoinder.

A batchelor says that if you hand a lady a
newspaper with a scrap out of it not a line will bo
read, but every bit of interest the paper pos-
sesses will be centred in finding out what the
missing scrap contained.
A Frenthman, wishing to spoakof the cream of
the English. poels, forgot the word, and said,
"Do butter of poets."

Pope, when he first saw Garrick act, observed,
"I am afraid that the young man will be spoiled,
for he will have no competitor 1"

A reporter upon a Western paper, speaking of a
certain noted beauty, remarked that the "pro-
fusion and colour of her hair would lead one to
look upon it as though it was spun by nimble
fingers of the easy hours as they glided through
the bright June days, whose sunny rays of light
were caught in the meshes, and were content to
go no further." The girl had red hair; that was
all.

When Baron Martin was at the Bar and ad-
dressing the Court of Exchequer in an insurance
case, he was interrupted by Mr. Baron Alderson
observing, "Mr. Martin, do you think any office
would insure your life P Remember, yours is a
brief existence."

A philosopher being' asked of whom he had
acquired so much knowledge, replied, " Of tho
blind, who do not lift their feet until they hays
first sounded, with their stick, the ground on which
they are going to tread."
A glorious bull is related in the life of Dr.
Sims of , a countryman of his, an Irishman, for
whom he had prescribed an emetic, who said with
great naivete, "My doer doctor, it is of no use
your giving me an emetic! I tried it twice in
Dubin, and it would not stay on my stomach either
time."

A spendthrift said, "Five years ago I was not
worth a farthing in the world; now see where I
am throvgh my own exertions." "Well, where
are you P" inquired a neighbour. "Why, I now
owe more than a thousand pounds!"

In former days, when roads were bad, and
wheeled vehicles almost unknown, an old laird
was returning from a supper patty, with his lady
mounted behind him on horseback. On crossing
the river Urr, the old lady dropped oif, but was
not mused till her husband reached his door.
The party who were despatched in quest of her,
arrived just in time to find her remonstrating
with the advancing tide, which trickled into her
mouth, in these words, "No anither drop; neither
het nor could." .

A retired cheesemonger, who hated any allusions
to the business that had enriched him, said to
Charles Lamb, in course of discussion on the Poor-
Laws, "You must -bear in mind, air, that I have
got rid of that sort of stuff which you poets call
the of human kindness.'" Lamb looked at
him steadily, and replied, "Yes I am aware of
that—you turned it all into cheese several years
ago!"

Norfolk, observed upon a board at a house by tho
roadside, the following strange inscription :—" A
goes koored hear." "How is it possible," &Lid
Rigby, "that such people as these can core
agues ?" "I do not *know," replied Garrick,
"what their prescription is—but it is not by a
spell."

doctor's. One day an elderly gentleman of the
foggy school blundered into the wrong shop.
"Dr. X-in ?" "Don't live here," says P-,
who was in full scribble over some important
papers, without looking up. "Oh I thought this
was his office." "Next door." "Pray, air can
you tell me, has the doctor many, patients?"
"Not living!" The old gentleman was never
'more heard of in the vicinity. ,

plagiarisms. They did little else than nudge eaoh
other as one amazing crib succeeded another,
until one whispered :—" Look at him! I declare
his very whiskers are curving into inverted
commas, and his face looks one entire quotation."

Mansion House, on Tuesday, July 23rd, 1872.

THE RIGHT HON. THE LORD MAYOR HI the Chair.

1. Proposed by the Right Hon. the Lord Mayor, seconded
by the Right Hon. Lord Lyttelton, and carried unani-
mously—
" That this Meeting having had placed before it a Pro-
spectus for the utilization of the Alexanira Park and
Palace, in the true interests of the Peosple, morally as well
as physically, pledges itself to every legitimate effort to
ensure the prompt and complete success of the enterprise."
2. Proposed by Sir John Bennett, Sheriff of London,
seconded by W. D. Christie, Esq., 0.8., and carried
unanimously—
" That the plan, suggested in the Prospectus produced,
of enabling the people to become themselves the pur-
chasers of the Park deserves the greatest encouragement,
and this Meeting pledges itself to give the movement its
most strenuous support."
3. Proposed by the Rev. Septimus Hansard, Ikt A.,
seconded by the Rev. Henry Solly, and carried unani-

mously :
"That this meeting desires to recommend to the active
co-operation of the churches of all deno ninations in the
metropolis an enterprise which, by promoting the rational
amusement and healthy recreation of tho people, will
greatly tend also to promote their moral and physical
welfare."

George Cruikshank, Esq., and earned unanimously
"That the following noblemen and gentlemen be re-

JOHN BULL PAYING THE PIPER.
THE Geneva award will for some time
furnish food for dissuasion to our politicians,
who hitherto have not displayed much wisdom
in relation to this matter, whilst our "Bold
Britons," our thorough " JonN BULLS" will
rail roundly at the pusillanimity of old Eng-
land in accepting a decision which, when
translated into ordinary phraseology, simPlY
means, "knuckle down" and "fork out."
The position the country ii placed in by this
Geneva decision is not a pleasant one, nay, it
is most vexatious and unpleasant. The vexa-
tion and unpleasantness, however, are not in
the fact that we have to pay money for wrong
done; but that we did the wrong with the
approval and loud applause of the " Bold
Britons and JOHN BULLS," who now strut
about with their noses in the air talking big
and looking foolish.
Lord PALMERSTON was a "great statesrnall
but in this matter he was slightly out in hil3
calculations. Earl RUSSELL iS a g‘ veteran
reformer," only he acted like a very stupid,
wrong-headed reactionary in relation to the Ala-
bama. case. Mr. Lunn is still member for
Birkenhead, and was, in his day, a very spirited
and enterprising British shipbuilder, who, in
pushing his own fortunes, was not bound to
be too nice either in regard to the honour or
the interests of the country. What these moll
did at the time, bad and foolish as it was, our
upper and our middle classes booked them UP
in. Earl RUSSELL, groping with his ere
shut for the onus probandi, was cheered to the
echo by middle and upper class "J'

BULLS and Bold Britons." Lord PALMER-

STON'S jaunty jokes were highly relished; and
Mr. LAIRD'S enterprise everywhere praised.
These "Bold Britons" hated slavery, but
they admired beyond measure the chivalry of
the slave.holders. They disliked very muoli
the Yankees, and they hoped for a separation
of the States, which would enfeeble a great
friendly empire, and leave with them the curse
of slavery as a bone of contention over which
they might fight for ever like hungry dogs.
When the Alabama went out it was cheered.
Every account sent to England of its ravages
after its escape was matter of rejoicing to the
"Joint BULLS and Bold Britons." These
highly respectable people were too busy with
their prejudices and their hatreds to take
time to think. When anybody hinted that
their conduct was calculated to interfore with
the safety of the ocean highways, they
laughed, and when certain working class
politicians declared that the day would cer-
tainly come when they would have to pay in
hard cash for their wretched folly, they
screamed with indignation, and repudiated the
thought of such a thing as a humiliation to
which the true "Jolts BULL" and world-
renowned " Bold Briton" never
_could sub-
mit.

Does not every man remember, too, how
the leading papers behaved on that ooeasion ?
Who can forget those fine descriptive and
wonderfully prophetic letters in the columns
of the Times, those vitriolic outpourings from
special correspondents at New York, Phila-
delphia and Washington, which seemed
written not so much to instruct the British
public as to " rile " the Yankees? Then
there was the Telegraph, justifying by its pre-
tentious smartness the old familiar similitude
brisk as a flea and ignorant as dirt ;"
and, to say nothing of the smaller fry, the
Standard overflowing with the drunken
ribaldry of "Manhattan" and kindred
spirits.

Then, in Parliament, had we not any
number of "Bold Britons" making history
for us, with Mr. R9EBUCK in the middle,
sententiously insulting to America from a
"JonN BULL" point of view? Had we not,
in fact, a thousand sickening evidences of the
folly and madness which, during the whole
course of the American war, characterized our
middle and upper classes, as well as that
portion of the newspaper press by which they
were represented? And—we put it with
pride—had we not all this time, though pain-
fully suffering for want of work, for lack of
food, had. we not our brave and honest
working men standing fiercely face to face with
this disgraceful, dishonest, and most unpa-
triotic baseness? Had it not been for the
patriotic, decided, and high-minded views
of our workers at that trying moment, it is
not the damages of a plundering Ala-
bama we should now have to pay, but the
heavy costs of a suicidal war. Not three or
three and a half millions, but millions counted
by the score, perhaps by the hundred, and
more fatal still our national honour and
national position would have gone into the bar-
gain. We say deliberately that at that trying
lnoment the working men of England saved
England from the loss of everything it is our
duty to cherish as a :nation. The attitude of
our working men at that trying time took from
that shameful Alabama raid the character of a
national not. It proved that our people at
heart were sound, and now that the settlement
has come and the money has to be paid it pre-
vents the transaction from carrying with it
the national humiliation that other wise would
have been inevitable.

It is a question worth enquiring into as to
whether or not in this case some way may not
be found by which this payment may be made
to fall on the shoulders of the guilty parties.
We are not in the habit now of calling on
treasonable or blundering statesmen to pay
With their heads; but there is no sufficient
reason why Earl RUSSELL should not be com-
pelled to do something with his purse. Mr.
LAIno cannot be hanged as a pirate; but the
fortune he made by his complicity with piracy
might be taken by the State as a slight
punishment for his wrong-doing. There are
hundreds, nay, thousands, of others in Liver-
pool and ol4ewhore, who onoourageg thin ixid

work, and grow rich on it; and they, not poor
working men, who always opposed it, ought to
be calleclbon to pay the fine imposed by the
Geneva award.

The working men of England will not, we
trust, be taken in by the swagger and loud
talk of "Bold Britons and JOHN BULLS," who
are simply gesticulating and looking ferocious
whilst humbly swallowing their leek. The
nasty thing has been forced into their mouths,
and there is nothing for them but to get it
down. There must be some relief, however,
in the thought that whilst they, as speculators
in rascality, got the profit, hardworking, poor
men will have to pay the cost. The nation
will carry the shame, and the blame, and
bear the expense; whilst members of both
Houses of Parliament, "great statesmen," and
others, with enterprising merebants, and such
as know how to turn the penny on a large
scale, will button their pockets, and protest
over their wino and cigars. Is it not time that
working men began to try whether in the
government of the nation they cannot trust
each other ?

articles.title: WORKING MEN CANDIDATES.
articles.text:
WORKING MEN CANDIDATES.

Mn. ODGER has nothing for it but to be
satisfied with such comments as the papers—
which are, in most cases, the organs of our
political parties—may think proper to make on
his public conduct. Whether he did right
in going to Preston we cannot say, simply be-
cause we do not know why he went there, nor
under what pressure of circumstances he left.
But, however, these matters may be explained.
We protest against the criticisms of the
Manchester Guardian, an acknowledged and
influential organ of the "great Liberal party,"
which, in the interest of its party, almost
raves against Mr. ODGEU for attempting to
"divide 'the Liberal interest. We have had
by far too much of this sort of thing, and if
such a stupid cuckoo note of more party, or
rather class trickery, be not changed, some day
or other the working men of England will
punish the policy which makes it necessary in
a most unmistakeable manner by dividing the
Liberal party so effectually as to put all
chance of re-uniting it again out of the ques-
tion.

If the "great Liberal party" was not bent
on its own destruction it would not so blindly
pursue its present policy in regard to the
representation of the country. There is
nothing more certain than that working men
chafe under their unfair exclusion from Parlia-
ment. They know there are questions of vital
interest to them continually before the Legisla-
ture, and except indirectly and as" outsiders,"
they have no voice in their settlement. They
are naturally anxious, therefore, that they
should have some small portion of direct repre-
sentation. But no sooner does a seat become
vacant in any of our popular constituencies
than some lawyer, who, as a ;rule, has himself
to look after, or some rich old retired manu-
facturer, who has made the acquiring of his
own fortune the Study of his life, thrust into it.
There is always some such claimant at hand
ready to take up the running, and no sooner
has the previous hero pulled up than the
"great Liberal party" flings its lawyer, or
old manufacturer, or some other self-seeking
or rich swell before the constituency; and
then, if a working-man candidate looks in to
see if there is any room for him, there is a
universal scream about dividing tho party and
letting in a Conservative. If such a game as
this goes on there will be nothing for it but to
divide the Liberal party. It will become the
duty of working men to utterly break it up if
it continues to act as a bar of exclusion to
them. We know that even if the Conserva-
tives got into power they could not remain
there without a Liberal policy, and an extreme
Radical party in the House, partly composed
of intelligent working men, would get more
out of them than can be forced from the Whigs
in the present condition of things.
There are several calculations of chances
which working men will have to make, and
when they have done this they may find it the
best policy for their interests to assist in
driving the present Government out into the
opposition. This will most certainly be
the case if working men candidates are not
encouraged and helped by the leaders and in-
fluelatiat friondt4 0 the "great Liberal party."

THE TIME WE LIVE IN.

THINGS are becoming serious. Very great
changes are impending. It is impossible that
matters should continue much longer as they
are. The difficulty of subsisting is growing
greater and greater every day. At present
there appears no way out of the wood. A
way, however, must be found, or the conse-
quences are terrible to think of. After that, or
after me, the Deluge, is a political saying
never more applicable than to the time we
live in. Well, if we are to have a social
flood, let us hope that in some ark of refuge
more than one family will find asylum. But,
for their admonition, let all ranks and classes
bear in mind that, though the waters en-
gulphed first the multitude of feeble folk
on the lower grounds, they ultimately reached
and swallowed up the last man who had
contrived to perch himself upon the loftiest
mountain.

A few indications of what is at
hand will be enough to name. The
price of coal having risen to what it did
in the hotest July on record, what may it not
be by Christmas, which, for all that weather
prophets can tell us for our comfort, may
bring us the severest December in our annals ?
The wheat harvest may prove tolerably plenti-
ful and good, and we know that, in some
countries of the world, it has been found both
excellent and abundant; yet, we see it esti-
mated, that, taking into consideration the
produce and the population of the entire globe,
the year's consumption will leave but little
over towards a second year's supply. Serious
as the Bakers' Strike may be under its own
proper aspect, we do not pretend to make it
one of the most formidable features in the
general picture. Every part, however, is rela-
tive, and, relatively, may easily have a greater
importance than is intrinsic to it. s'The failure,
for example, of the potato rep is, in this
view of it, an appalling circumstance. We
can no longer afford to eat meat, and the next
most universal article of dinner diet is going,
we are told, not to he eatable. Meanwhile,
rinderpest has broken out in Yorkshire, of
all counties in England ; and the price of
meat, instead of coming down, is quite
certain to rise yet higher.
The Imperial Parliament never broke up for
the long holidays under circumstances of
illor omen for the prospects of the country.
What, then, at such a moment, are we, as a
State and Government, doing? Playing at
soldiers on Salisbury Plain! Nothing more
grossly absurd an.' ill-timed was over seen.
Invasion! Why, is not our poverty coming
as one that travelleth, and our want as an
armed man? Everybody is astir to meet the
onoome in some way or other, some more,
others less; the only men among us that are
doing nothing, nothing but aeting to admira-
tion the part of SOLOMON'S sluggard, are the
very mon that ought to be up and doing; not
with folded arms, calling for more sleep and
slumber, but passing sleepless nights as well
as wakeful days to meet a cruel exigency,
assuage, if possible, an inevitable emergency,
and to avert a too possible and even probable
convulsion. How long wilt thou sleep, 0
sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy
sleep?

The only answer that we get to such appeals
is, that the season was very laborious, quite
exhausting, and by no means unproductive in
good and useful 'measures. Is it meant to be
told us that every thing and every person
must wait till February before the wheels of
Government can be set in motion towards
any purpose beyond those provided for by the
labours of the past Session? Granted that
the advantages of government by representa-
tion cannot be reaped but at the cost of waiting
for those Jong deliberations which spring
from the multitude of counsellors, and that,
therefore, if some subjects are dealt with
others must be deferred. Nevertheless, the
advocates of autocracy, government by a
single man, paternal government as they
love to call it, ought not to be allowed to
contrast the immediate action that a Sultan or
a Czar may take with the sullen inactivity of
a constitutional order of things under an
impending necessity and in the face of
threatening prospects.
The next eyaeioa by which aa appeal like

this is attempted to be shirked is to reply
that the country is in a highly prosperous
condition, almost never better off. It is use-
less, however, to talk of prosperity to a
people who may see, yet cannot feel it. This
is trifling with millions as the old fable
trifles with the individual TAxraiars, who,
also, had abundance under his eyes, but
always kept beyond his reach. We may not
deny that many branches of trade are now in
such a state as rapidly to fill the pockets and.
purses of the capitalists. As a mere matter
of fact we are likewise bound to admit that in
-various directions wages are higher than they
were at former times. But what signifies
that if the week's wages now reSeived will
not buy half as much to eat, drink, and cook
with as the lower rate of payment for men's
earnings used to do?
In short, the facts are so plain and, so
pressing, that our statesmen, close beset, will
turn to bay. What, they will cry out im-
patiently, what would you have ? Perhaps, at
the first, there may seem some vagueness,
incoherency, and even wildness, about the
answers given. Men cannot but feel that
which severely pinches thorn; and, when the
pinch becomes hard, they must cry out. And. are
they not entitled to relief, unless they can tell
quite certainly, quite calmly, and quite clearly
what would relieve them ? Is their impor-
tunity disposed of, got rid of, if they ask ;for
the wrong thing, or for too many things,
or for a selection of things that can, not
simply not be granted all at once, but perhaps
may conflict with one another?
One fancies, that were he responsible for the
safe and satisfactory conduct of publics affairs,
two sounds which, among many others, pro-
ceed from voices like the sound of many
waters, would. make distinct impressions upon
the drums of his ears.

Are we deceived in supposing that we hear
such cries as "Down with the Game Laws,"
and "Down with the Land Laws." Well, as to
the first, it may be a moot point, whether the
repeal of these statutes which authorise and
uphold the preservation of game for the sport of
the rich, would be a panacea for the complaints
of the poor. But the famine prices to which
articles of diet commonly termed necessaries of
life have risen, seem to be the one thing
needful to complete that condemnation of those
selfishly instituted statutes already pronounoed
over and over again by a public opinion so broad
as to include all but the interested few, with
not a small proportion even of themselves.
With beef and mutton at upwards of a
shilling a pound, it will not much longer be
endured, that for a hungry man to catch a
partridge or a hare and eat it, shall expose
him to the same disgrace and penalty as if he
had perpetrated a base and dishonest theft.
To speak of the Land Laws opens a wide
question; but the proper function of the land
on which a people are born and reared, is to
produce food for their subsistence, and there can
be no right of individual property in the soil,
which interferes with—nay, which does not
subserve—this first, indefensible, and most
sacred purpose.

articles.title: CARL MARX ON WORKING MEN LEADERS.
articles.text:
CARL MARX ON WORKING MEN
LEADERS.

THE session (if the International on Tues-
day afternoon began with the ease of Citizen
BARRY, who is a Scotch boot and shoe dealer,
upon which a warm discussion ensued. This
dispute was ended by MARX, who declared
with much warmth that all of the professed
leaders of the working men in England were
unworthy of confidence; that they were,
more or less, sold to the GLADSTONES, the
MORLEYS, and the DuxEs ; that it was no
honour to belong to them, but a shame ; and
that Citizen BARRY was infinitely superior in
every moral qualification to any of them.
This is not a very flattering statement as
far as the London loaders of our working people
are concerned. It would be unfair to assert that,
after a residence of some years in England,
CARL MARX knows nothing of London work-
ing men and their leaders. He must have an
acquaintanee more or less extensive with
them. We presume, however, that the most
intimate part of it lies amongst those who have
joined themselves to him as members of tho
luteriuktioual Society. Whother tho gentle'

men named have purchased these, or any
number of them, Mr. CARL Mira may have
an opportunity of knowing; possibly he may
be able to name the exact price in pounds,
shillings, and pence; he may, also, be able to
name those amongst his English associates
who have received the money, as no doubt his
ears are made the receptacles of many dis-
creditable secrets. We have no hesitation,
however, in asserting that his cook-and-bull
story about the sale and purchase mentioned
is simply the result of his own disturbed
dreams. Continental politicians are com-
monly afflicted with a diseased suspicion.
They cannot imagine an honest human
intercourse. The prime duties of life,
in their eyes are spying, betraying, bribing.
CARL MA-ax is evidently afflicted with this
Continental itch, without suspecting what a
loathsome thing it is, or without reflecting
that perhaps the gentlemen named would not
consider his friends worth buying. To what
profitable use could any honest sensible man
turn such persons Moen, in the "Vicar
of Wakefield," with his gross of green spec-
tacles, was rich in a worldly sense, compared
to what any respectable man would be
with a dozen such peasons as am
MAts. alludes to. If Mr. Moerst or Sir
CTIARLES DILKE, or anybody else was foolish
enough to buy them, they would be gin-d to
sell them again as soon as possible at a con-
siderable discount, or, like DOGRatRY'S watch,
allow them to steal out of their company.
We have no hesitation whatever in telling
CARL MARX that his language, as applied to
leading Working men, has no truth whatever
in it in anygeneral sense, and as applied to the
gentlemen named it is simply a libellous in-
sult. The policy of removing the Interna-
tional to New York might, when discussed at
the Hague, be open to certain objections on the
part of itsimembers in England; now, however,
wo imagine that even its best friends in
England willbe convinced thatthe further it is
off the better—especially if in its emigration
CARL MARX, its chief, should be included.

THE OPERATION OF THE BALLOT.
TAR Conservatives, at a local country
election, have been placing their under strap-
pers outside the voting-place, to mark off the
names of the men who had voted as they oamo
out. They must be made welcome to What-
ever information or consolation, the process
may yield them. It is of more general and more
legitimate interest to learn from the testimony
of the returning officer at Pontefract, how the
method of secret voting, first tried under his
superintendence, operated in that fine old
borough. There was a kind of poetical beauty
as well as justice in making the experiment
where, to accommodate a strong phrase,
SALAMIS seat used to be.

As the Mayor's memory enables him to
testify, election times were formerly marked
by scenes of violence and floods of drunken-
ness. On this occasion, there was an entire
absence of apparent political excitement, and
not one instance of misconduct or complaint
of any kind came before the magistrates as a
concomitant or consequenee of the election.
No difficulty was found in taking the votes.
Those electors who could read were from half
a minute to forty seconds about it, and found
the vehole process surprisingly simple. That fewer
voted than usual veas to be accounted for by
other causes than the newness of the method.
In 1868, there was a four months' canvass;
in 1872, the canvass lasted but three, or, at
most, four days. Besides this, many of the
electors, being adverse to a contest, abstained
from voting. The local militia were out in pros-
pect of the Autumn Manceuvres ; and the Knot-
.
tingley men, many of whom are sailors, who
were at home in the winter of 1868, were out
it sea in the summer of the present year.

With respect to counting the votes, Mr.
310XON'S report is equally satisfactory. A
number of the papers were found a*kwardly
folded, and took more time to open out; and
there was delay from the care taken to keep
the endorsed figures from the keen eyes of
electioneering agents. Nevertheless, he is of
opinion that from 750 to a thousand can be
disposed of in an hour. The chief difficulty
was with those who could not read. These,
however, will diminish in number every year.
In the Meantime, the declaration they have to

make might be much simplified, and, the
fourteen blanks which the proper clerk has
now to fill up, might be got rid of by having
the declarations made on one sheet at each
booth, with but two blanks, one for name and
number, and the other for the mark. It is a
circumstance of interest at least, if not of im-
portance, that the MAYOR, who has Veen
returning officer at three elections, was, even
at the last, an opponent of the Ballot, but
has been converted by his expereinee of its
smooth and satisfactory working.

THE USE AND ABUSE OF LEISURE.
THE New York 117/Won views with extreme
disfavour the final triumph of the eight hour
system in nearly all the trades in that city.
Though we cannot for a moment endorse the
opinion that because a man may make a bad
use of leisure, therefore he should be com-
pelled to forego the right to that which alone
prevents him from degenerating into a mere
machine, there is no more harm in looking at
the side of the question presented by this un-
sympathetic journal.
Whether the shortening of his hours of
labour is a benefit to a man or not, says
the Nation, depends partly on the means
i by which the shortening s procured and
partly on the man's own character. In the
not very encouraging account given the other
day, by the commandant of the Rock Island
Arsenal, of the result of the eight-hour system
there, it appeared that the extent to which
the men turned their increased leisure to good
account depended on their moral and mental
training. The higher classes of mechanics
profited by it; the masons did so to some ex-
tent; but to the common labourers it was
sltaply a source of injury botli to health and
morals. Therefore, before we can tell whether
a man's condition is likely to be improved by
having his day's work shortened, we have to
find out what kind of man he is; and if we
test the vain, of the succ'ess of the movement
in this city in this way, we fear the prospect
will not be found to be very cheering. The
great body of the younger mechanics who are
foremost in the agitation have not received
the kind of trainin,,,,, and are not in the state
of mind, to make them very likely, to use the
newly-acquired two hours for their own real
benefit. The present writer had occasion, a
few months ago, to witness the working bf two
elderly carpenters, bred in the old American
school, on a very nice job, side by side with
two younger ones of the:new, noisy, rhetorical,
agitating school. The seniors were model
Workmen, faithful, punctual, and industrious,
although working under a boss's contract, at
a distance from the shop; and keenly interested
in their work, and sensitive to the last degree
about its excellence. The juniors came an
hour later than they every day, and went off
to the nearest grocery every day, some days
as many as five times, to get drinks, and were
invariably fretful and querulous, dis-
gusted with the job, and. anxious to quit it
when it , presented. difficulties which only
seemed to rouse the older men's ardour. On
enquiry, we found that the latter belonged to
no union, never had oared nothing about the
eight-hour movement, and did not believe any
first-class carpenters were in it; while the
juniors Were apparently leaders.
Now, we think it may be laiddown as a rule,
that repose which a man extorts or gets for
nothing is if not hurtful, of little benefit to
him. Inherited leisure is generally a curse,
whir.,bh only strong characters can escape;
and so is leisure won by gambling or lucky
speculation. "Well-won repose," as it is
called—that is, the repose earned by hard.
work, or taken, as the vacation of most
workers with the brain is taken, simply as a
means of qualifying one's self to work more
effectively thereafter—is, indeed, on the whole,
the only repose by which the race /las gained
anything. If the working-men sought leisure
for these reasons and in this spirit, society
would undoubtedly gain by their having it,
and so would they themselves. If, for in-
stance, carpenters were as deeply interested in
carpentry, or masons in masonry, as lawyers
are in the law, doctors in medicine, and
ministers in the ministry, and longed to
excel in it and perfeat themselves in it more
and more, it would not be possible to lengthen
their evenings and diminish their purely
muscular toil by two hours without greatly
increasing their power of doing gad, honest
work. They would use their leisure to perfect I
themselves in one way or another in their
trades. But if it be true, as we believe it is,
that the great body of those engaged in this
movement look on their callings as simply
repulsive forms of toil, in which stern neces-
sity compels them to submit, but which
every man is justified in escaping by any
means within his reach, and in putting
pout
of his mind as well as out of his
sight as soon as he lays downs his tools, it
would be very, rash to look for any better re-
sults from itthan a diminution of production,
a transfer of industry to other places, and an
increase of extrayttgance, drinking, and other

forms of demoralization among the working
men.

In fact, we have no hope that the eight-hour
system will be of much value to the working
men, except under the co-operative s'qtern.
As long as it comes in the form of a yiotory
won over the greedy bosses, -with huzzas and
wavings of hats, it cannot do permanent good.
When it comes by the deliberate resolution of
the men themselves, after mature considera-
tion of what it will cost them in production,
and with full knowledge that it will cost them
something—as it would come if it came
through the vote of the co-operative society—
it is pretty sure to result in better work,
better health, better morals, and greater
happiness.
The want of interest the nation supposes
working men to take in their peculiar em-
ployments (which, if true, would be explained
by the mechanical nature of their work) is about
the strongest argument that could be brought
forward in proof of the necessity of their
securing leisure for the cultivation of pursuits
which like those of " lawyers " and "minis-
ters" have the power of interesting intelligent
human beings.

articles.title: MAKING A LIVING.
articles.text:
MAKING A LIVING.

AZA.MAT BLTuk, writing in the Examiner,
expresses some of the "strange thoughts
which are suggested to a foreign mind when
meditating upon cheapness of life and dear
ness of living." Life, he says, is cheap in
this country in the economical sense, inso-
much that its supply far, exceeds the
demand, and cheap in a less scientific sense,
because an inhabitant of the British Islands
will undergo almost anything on the chance
of getting a living. Are there, he asks, many
English, Scotch, or Irish men who venture to
hope for more than bare living, even in their
dreams ? Yet the country's boast is that its
industry advances "not by steps, but by
strides; not by strides, but by leaps and
bounds." AZAJAAT BATUK then observes that
BO do.the prices of coals, meat and potatoes,
and. continues as follows :

Foreigners have, strictly speaking, nothing
to say to all this. We get excellent cotton ware,
magnificent m achines, capital cutlery, and beau-
tiful breeds of horses and cattle from people who
report themselves to be the richest, the freest,
and the best governed. We can only be
grateful, and express regret at being unable to
do as much and to say as much of ourselves.
But when occasionally we come over here' to
see how you manage to secure all these busses,
our whole conception of these islands roman-
tically hidden in nebulto is ()hanged from top
to bottom. We soon perceive what it means.
to manufacture some one else's cotton, instead
of manufacturing one's own silk, wool, or
grapes. We soon begin to believe that as a
matter both of prospective and of present
Fosperity and comfort it is muchimore safe
to take advantage of our iron and coals in our
own slow way, than in the rapacious and
feverish one of yours. We soon see that tbe
splendid race-horses and prize animals you
send us over, to improve by-and-by our
breeds, are produced at the cost of half your
population not tasting meat more than once a
week, if at all. And just as soon do we feel
that, though reluctant to boast that as a
nation we are rich, or free, or well governed,
each of us individually is incomparably More
independent and prosperous with his little
plot of land or his tidy purse than the vast
majority of you are with your increased
Saturday's wages representing the reward of
a week's contribution to the progress of the
glorious industry.

articles.title: KENILWORTH IN 1872.
articles.text:
KENILWORTH IN 1872.

Who but:a wealthy English nobleman can in-
dulge in the: Juxury of nursing the decrepitude of
a shapeless ruin, and letting seven acres of land
lie untilled ? That
.some:are to be found at the
present time who are rendering this service to
mouldering walls and mounds of earth is in itself,
in the eyes of archeologists, a sufficient justifica-
tion of the peerage. But the English public is
not without its obligations to these same nobles;
for were it not for them how seldom would John
Bull see with his bodily eyes the actual records of
the great past of this country, and in all proba-
bility we should not be able to take our/stand with
quiet pleasure in the base-court of ruined Kenil-
worth. We owe our thanks, then, to the Earl of
Clarendon for the very evident care that is con-
stantly bestowed upon all that remains of Kenil-
worth Castle. .We could wish that there were
fewer printed notices posted on the walls to -warn
the climbers off them—fewer spikes and rails at
every turn and corner—a less evident prepara-
tion for the reception of excursionists. But, above
all, we wish the disfiguring additions of modern
inasonry, especially where they take auornamental
form, quite uncalled for and moat unwelcome to
the eye that dwells with interest upon the old
itortowork, The architectural value Of the ruins

SEPT. 14, 187.

is not great, and cannot for a moment be compared
withrheir historic worth. Only in the ruins of
the great hall, in its grand porch, in its windows,
and in its beautiful oriel, is an approach to refined
architectural detail to be discovered, and even here
its di itinetness is obliterated by long exposure'
and by reason of the soft nature of the reddish
sandstone of which the hall is built. The arehi-
tectural student will find, then, little here to fill,
his sketch-book. The rains are too essentially

picturesque and shadowy to afford many deter-
minate features for him to seize upon. ' The
artist, with his colours, is the proper person here ;-
but for him how many charming and affecting
subjects are presented in the great circuit of what
remains of Kenilworth.—Builder.

THE REPRESENTATION OF PRESTON.

The nomination of candidates for the vacancy in
the parliamentary representation of Preston took
place on Tuesday. The required period of two
hours appointed for the purpose was between noon
and two o'clock, during which time the Mayor
(Myles Myres, Esq.), as returning officer, Was in
attendance at the Town Hall, with Mr. Ashcroft,
the town clerk. A few minutes after twelve
o'clock the two rival candidates, who have been
before the constituents for s'ome days, were formally
proposed. The Liberal candidate, Mr. James
German, of Vine Court, Sevenoaks, Kent, Wee
nominated by Mr. D. Irvine, and Emended by Mr. J.
Goodier. His nomination was countersigned by
several gentlemen. The Conservative candidate,
Mr. J. Holker, Q.C, described as of Devonshire-
street, Portland-place, London, was nominated by
Mr. Edmund Birley, seconded by Mr. John Raw-,
&Hie, and to his nomination there were appended
the names of other gentlemen. No other can-
didate was proposed.

_
The election took place on Friday, but tho
result was not known when we went to press.

THE INTERNATIONAL.

The Congress of the Internationalists at the
Hague closed on Saturday night. On Friday
there was a public sitting of a very tumultuous
character, and the uproar prevented the coniinuance
of the debate. At the close of the sitting there
was a public demonstration against the principles
of the Society. The " public " struck up the
National Anthem," and the members of the
Congress:replied by chaunting the " Marsoillaise."
The proceedings must have been extremely edi-
fying, and nobody was surprised to learn on Satur-
day that six delegates had left in high dudgeon.
They assign as the reason for their departure that
they were unable to bring about the political or-
ganisation of the International Society, and that
they were adverse to the transfer of the General
Council to the United States. The telegrams state
that at the secret sitting on Friday it was re-
solved that the Council shall be removed
from London to New York. The faction
opposed to Marx numbered at the final test
22 members. They embraced all the London
malcontents, one of the Americans, part of the
Swiss, all the Belgians, all the Dutch, and the
Spanish representatives from Valencia. These 22
members have resolved to cut loose from the
organisation, and to set up another one for them-
selves, expecting to be joined by all the Inter-
nationalists in Italy and Russia. No delegates
from these two countriea were present at the
Congress.

articles.text:
REVIEWS.

THE ROMANCE OF PEASA.NT LIFE IN TIIE
WEST OF ENGLAND. By FRANCIS GEORGE
HEATH (Cassell, Petter, and Galpin, La
Belle Sauvage-yard, Ludgate•bill).

This book is—on- a subject of deep interest to
every section of English society, and one
which has yet to play a great part in the
future of this country. The question of the
improvement of the oondition of our agri-
cultural labourers is now fairly before the
public, and Mr. Heath, in the volume before
us, contributes his observations of their de-
gradation in one of the most lovely and fertile
counties of England, viz., Somersetshire.

A graphic description of the journey on the
great Western unfolds the sphere of Mr.
Heath's explorations. "The fine old county"
of Somerset was his destination, the labourers'
homes in that county the places from whence
ho gathered materials for his work. A curious
incident introduces him to the hero of a story
of which the briefest of outlines is alone possi-
ble—a poor Somersetshire boy, now a pros-
perous London tradesman—a lad sent to work
at four a.m., with a mere mouthful of bread
for breakfast and some sour cider, hunting the
hedges for snails, which he had to eat in order
to stop the cravings of hunger ; and, after a
day's work, "weak, hungry, and exhausted,
returning to a supper, to be partaken of by
nine besides himself, consisting of three or
four spoonfuls of flour and the rest water."
The children often sent to bed hungry, in
order that in the obliviousness of sleep they
might find a temporary relief from:the crav-
ings of their unsatisfied appetites. George
Mitchell, of Montacute, is he to whom the
writer refers; but there are many such. " Seven
shillings a week for wages, and is. 6d. a
week for his cottage," is the account of one
who had worked hard on that munificent sum
nearly all his life. John P. is another. A
house seven yards long, three wide, height of
walls not six feet. No second floor, the
ground irregularly paved with large stones,
with earth between and in their crevices.
Wages ss. a week. Out of that £2 10s. a
year rent for his "cottage," and Ns. a year
more for the privilege of running his pig.

But why mention more; the book is full of
them, and every one ought to know that
hitherto the labourer has neither had proper
wages nor-a decent cottage. The present agita-
tion has already raised his wages; the Union
when established will place him in the secure
enjoyment of good wages, so that he can live
as a human being ought to live. lie can de-
pend with safety upon nothing else—the
Union will be his best security for the future;
and if the labourer should stop short in the
noble work now commenced, he will un-
doubtedly regret it.
The book, which is published at one shilling,
is well worthy of the careful perusal of all
who take an:interest in the elevation of the
tillers of the soil.

THE CAUSES OP SOCIAL REVOLTB.—A Lecture
by CAPT. KusE, R.N. Longman, Green,

Reader, and Dyer.
All men desirous to see such controversies
as our political and social condition may lead
to in the future, conducted profitably, should
read this excellent pamphlet. Captain Mane
treats his subject very fully, and in all he has
to say sustains himself by the quotation of
numerous authorities. Nothing could be better
than the spirit in which certain very ticklish
points are handled, general prejudices being
exposed and ordinary practices called in ques-
tion with a seriousness and sincerity of tone
impossible for any but the most bigoted to find
fault with. It is not necessary here to go
into an examination of the several
points taken up and discussed by
the lecturer. The questions he raises
and handles so admirably must have,
before they arc settled, a very full disoussion,
and if all who take part in these discussions
Possess the same largeness of view and toler-
ance of spirit as Captain Manse, the best
results may be looked for. His remarks on
the influence of the daily press deserve serious
consideration. Nothing can be worse than the
Way in which our most influential journals
treat public potions connected with the con-

duet and progress of the working people. Indeed
working men's questions and working men's
proceedings are always either left out of sight
altogether, or travestied until their pressure
on Parliament, or on some strong established
interest, forces public attention to them, and
then only our newspapers think them worthy
of even the most passing notice.
We give the Captain's " Platform" as
more profitable for thought in the present
state of the public mind than anything of a
like kind at present before the public :-
1. Compulsory, gratuitous, secular educa-
tion.
2. Land Tenure Reform.
3. Substitution of direct for indirect
taxation.

4. Electoral representative reform.
There is enough here to think about for
some time to come.

articles.title: WORK AND WAGES OF THE LONDON POSTMEN.
articles.text:
THE WORK AND WAGES OF THE
LONDON POSTMEN.

PART 11.

After they are stamped, the letters are passed on
to the sorting tables. There, is, firstly, the general
sorting, by which the letters are divided into
town, suburban, and country. Each of these
divisions are then taken off to be further sub-
divided; the town and suburban into districts or
sections, the country into divisions and "roads."
A "road" is the technical term for a given
number of towns on the same line of rail, for each
of which a separate bag is made up, and left by
the Mail Guard, in most cases without stopping
the train. This is done by a mechanical con-
trivance attached to the sorting carriage, which
will, at one motion, leave one bag and take up
another.

Dispatching a road from the General Post Office
is a very responsible duty, as the letters arc tied
in bundles containing one or two hundred, and
when one of these bundles is accidentally placed
in the wrong bag, the delay is very serious. The
sorter, too, has to attend to all unpaid letters,
frequently several pounds' worth, in small sums
of twopence or fourpenee ; and also to see that the
Registered Letter-Bag, for which Ito signs a
receipt, is properly placed in the bag. All this
must be done with the utmost rapidity, the vans
starting for the railway at a stated time, and a
delay even of a minute or two rarely occurs.
The town letters undergo a very similar process.
They are first sorted into East Central, West
Central, Northern, Western, &0., and these are
immediately dispatched by carts to their respective
districts.

The East Central division, which is the one
delivered from the General Post Office, is then sub-
divided into let, 2nd, and 3rd sections, which are
again sorted into walks, the number at this office
being fifty-two.
They now come into the hands of the letter
carrier who is to deliver them, and w ho has to
arrange them in such a manner that he may not
have to run backwards and forwards on his walk,
or go twice to the same house. This, of course,
is but a continuation of the sorting process. They
are first "thrown off," that is, each street is
separated, and firms which do a large business by
letter are placed by themselves. They are then
"set in," that is, placed in such a manner that
the streets, and the numbers in the street, follow
each other in the order in which the letter-carrier
intends to work his walk. This being done, and
the "Charge" (unpaid letters) booked to the
various names whore it will be left, the whole are
tied in bundles, placed carefully in a bag sb that
the bundle first wanted will appear at the top, and
so on; the letter•carrier is then ready for his
delivery.
It is now about half-past seven, and he sallies
forth to distribute his letters t@ the public. This
takes him from an hour to an hour and a half, and
as soon as he has finished, he goes to the nearest
Receiving House (Post-office) and gets the post-
master to sign a printed card, in which are stated
the times of despatch, of leaving the office, com-
mencement, and finish of delivery. This the
letter-carrier also signs, and gives up to the charge-
taker when he attends the office for his second
delivery. There are many incidents of an amus-
ing, and not a few of an annoying nature oo-
curring to the postman on delivery. There arc
some people who evidently
,think that ho is, or
ought to be omniscient with respect to the streets
of London and the people who live in them. A
man on duty in the City is frequently asked where
such and such a street at Notting-hill or Bays-
water is; or at what number in that street Mr.
C. or Mr. D. will be found; and the inquirer
seems totoniehed when told that he doe,' not know.

He is constantly pestered with questions, as to
the time of despatch or arrival of the various
mails, when a letter will be delivered if posted
at a certain time, the commercial character or
respectability of people on his walk, &0., &c.
Sometimes, his knock being heard in a street, he
will he called a distance of twenty or thirty yards
only to be asked whether he has a letter for Mr.
W., or whether such and such a mail is in. The
Irish who swarm our City courts and alleys are
particularly amusing. Perhaps the letter-carrier
has a letter for Dennis M'Carthy, Frying-pan-
alley, without a number. Well, he goes there,
and is immediately surrounded by the men and
women, all speaking at once in a rich brogue,
which makes them all but unintelligible. "Is it
Mike Donavon ?" asks one; "Is it from Limerick ? "
asks another; a third says, "There's no M'Carthy
hero, but if you go to Misther Jones maybe he'll
tell ye." The poor fellow turns away in despair,
but questions and suggestions are rained down
upon him from all sides, and from every door and
window in the court; whilst a troop of little
rugged urchins surround his feet, each begging
for the bit of string with which his letters are
tied, and, if refused, greeting him with observa-
tions more personal than polite; and, perhaps,
failing to get what they want, presenting him
with various articles which he does not require,
such as mud, orange-peel, and even stones and
brickbats. These are trifles, but they are apt to
try the patience even of a postman.
(To be continued.)

A Birmingham gentleman has just received
a letter from Australia, in which it is stated
that large quantities of tin have recently been
discovered, and that all the "Men upon the
Station are tin mad." The discovery has been
made upon the Strathbogie Run, 15 miles from
Wellingrove, and 90 from Armadale, in New
South Wales.

The Non/ announces that a duel with
swords has taken place on the Belgian frontier,
between Baron de Levey and Vicomte
d'llordylla, a wealthy Spaniard, and formerly
an officer of the Carlist army. The latter
was severely wounded, and with great difll.•
°tiny carried to an hotel at Courtrai, where he
is in the midst of several Carlist officers.

The reernitinr, for the Royal Engineers, does
not go on briskly, owing to the large amount
of employment, especially for skilled artisans.

The late Mr. James Garrett Frost has be-
queathed legacies to various Manchester
charities to the amount of £20,100. Of this
sum .£5,000 is given to the Manchester In-
firmary, and £3,000 to the Salford Dispensary.

At the Bilston Police-court on Tuesday,
Thomas Jones, a miner, from Sedgley, was
sent to gaol for two months for severely
chastising his son, a child five years of age.

Shortly after the close of the Autumn
Manceuvres his Royal Highness the Prince of
Wales is expected to visit Colchester for the
purpose of reviewing the 10th Hussars, prior
to the departure of that corps for India.

A Shetland Correspondent writes that
Captain Burton has just arrived in Lerwick in
the steamer Jon Sigurdsson, from Iceland,
whore he was engaged exploring the interior
of the island for two or three months.
Several other English travellers have also
arrived. Some of them made the ascent of
Heola, and all of them had to "rough it" a
good deal more than they expected. Captain
Burton leaves immediately for Italy to take
up the Consulship at Trieste, vacant by the
death of Mr. Charles Lever.

At the Marylebone Pollee-court on Wednes-
day an auxiliary letter-carrier was convicted
of drunkenness whilst upon duty. He was
fined £5, with the alternative of a month's
imprisonment.

A violent costermonger, who had ferociously
assaulted two women and a policeman, has becn
sentenced by the Lambeth police magistrate
to eighteen months imprisonment with hard
labour.

Much confusion and bloodshed have arisen
over the elections in Brazil, which have taken
place very greatly under military influence,
and without the participation of the Liberals,
who withdrew from the Contest

A gentleman of Swansea has been hoaxed
on the receipt of the following telegram :
G. IL Whalley to Crook, Swansea. Come
immediately to London by express, and Mr.
Whalley's carriage will be waiting for you at
Paddington station." The lion, member for
Peterborough attended at Bow-street on
Wednesday, to state that he knew nothing
whatever of the message thus sent in his
name, and the magistrate promised that if the
court could render any assistance in detecting
the offender it should be done.
