FRIDAY.

The English dispute at Geneva has net
yet been settled. The Rev. Mr. Downton
certainly preached last Sunday, but the
committee maintain the chaplain's dismissal
and merely allow him the use of the chapel
in deference to the Bishop of London.

The Emperor William of Prussia has ap-
pointed the Russian Field-Marshal and
tilovernor of Poland, Count Berg, to the com-
mand of the 52nd Prussian Regiment of
Infantry.

Mr. Lord, mpager of the Brighton Aqua-
rium, writes that two pair of beautiful speci-
mens of the paradise or peacock fish have
just been received there. This fish came first
from China.

The Kent Herald is authorised to state
that after the most rigid* and careful inquiry
no cause of the origin of the fire at Can-
terbury Cathedral has been discovered.
"Those who certainly are the best able to
form an opinion," it adds, "declare that it
did not originate with the plumbers ; but as
no other source of fire is acknowledged to,v
even suggested, the public are left to imagine a
me
i means for themselves, or they may place their
faith n that which each of them believes
most."

The Burmese Ambassadors arrived in Edin-
burgh yesterday.

As the first train from Kemble Junction
was entering the Cirencester Station, shortly
after nine o'clock yesterday morning, the
engine ran off the rails, but none of the
passengers in the train were injured.
•
A coroner's jury at Liverpool have returnea
a verdict of manslaughter against a boy named
Cloy, aged nine years, who killed another lad
about the same age while showing him bow
people were garotted.
In his address as member of the Jurispru-
dence and Amendment of the Law section at
the Social Science Congress, yesterday morn-
ing, Sir J. Coleridge promised, to do all be
could next session in the way of law reform,
but he warned the public not to expect too
much, as there were certain matters to which
the Government must give Precedence.

Five fires are mentioned in Captain Shaw's
official report yesterday, and in none of them.
was any great amount of damage done. In
one case a Jiro broke out from some undis-
covered cause in the ground floor of the
private house, 10, Gilston-road, West Bromp-
ton, occupied by Mr. C. Tracey. The flames
were confined to the parlour, which was burned
out, but all the other nine rooms in the house
suffered some injury.

The carman Spaull, who is in oustody for
having caused the death of a chill named
Wooden, by administering a quantity of pep-
per, under circumstances which bays been
already reported, is committed for trial on a
charge of manslaughter.

The bona Me traveller question was before
the Clerkenwell magistrate the other day,
when several licensed victuallers were charged
with having their houses open for the sale of
liquor during prohibited hours on a Sunday.
In each case the summons was dismissed.

There was another fire on Tuesday afternoon
on Tooting Beek Common, and about a quarter
of an acre of furze was. burned, There were
several other fires in London on Tuesday after-
noon, but the damage in each ease was only
The Birkenhead magistrates had before
them the other day a beerseller charged with
permitting drunkenness in his house. The
defendant denied the charge, stated that it was
throwing money away to get drunk, that he
never allowed money to be thrown away in his
house, that he had himself been a teetotaller all
his life, and that ho did not know what the
taste of drink was. The case was dismissed.

The Spener Gazette attributes to Prince
Bismarck a declaration to the effect that the
assembling of the monarchs is everywhere
regarded as the conclusion—guaranteeing
peace—of the late events.

The South Aindrioan news brought by the
Tasmania includes further details connected
with the important political events in Peru.
It appears that during the brief dictatorship
of the late Colonel Guitierez, his soldiers fired
a volley into the American Consulate, happily
without injuring any one, and that several
American naval officers were fired at while
embarking in boats. Marceline Guitterez, a
brother of the dictator, has been taken prisoner
on board a steamer, while trying to escape
from the country. Flo was disguised as a
Chinaman, and accompanied by his wife and
child.

Tho movement against the present high
price of meat has assumed a definite shape at
aaniey, A Co-operative Butchers' Society
has been started, and an average number of
shares has been taken up. The butchers are
acting on the tlefenßive and are limiting the
supply.

THE WEEK'S NEWS.

Dr. Cumming preached before the Queen
on Sunday at a private service in Dunr obin
Castle.

On Friday last tho Princess of Wales en-
tertained the whole Royal Family of Denmark
at dinner on board the yacht Victoria and
Albert.

The autumn mtinanivres have been of
much interest, and, after a sharp encounter,
the decision as to the tactical disposition
was in favour of the Southern army. On
Saturday evening the Prince of Wales was
entertained at a banquet at Salisbury, at
which the Duke of Cambridge, the Duke of
Teak, and several foreign officers of distinc-
tion were present.

Owing to the high price of coal the depres-
sion at Liverpool in the trade done by ocean-
going steamers continues. It is stated that
the cost of working a large steamer is now
£45 more per day than it was a few months
ago.

Under the new Act of Parliament for
facilitating the retirement of deans and
canons, the Dean of Winchester has given
notice that he intends to resign his office. Dr.
Gamier, who was a Fellow of All Souls'
College, Oxford, as far back as 1800, has held
the Deanery of Winchester, value £1,500 a
year, since 1810. From 1807 until 1868 the
very rev, gentleman was rector of Bishopstoke,
value £645 per annum.

Mr. Macpherson - Walls, who bad been
named as a candidate to succeed Mr. Brooke,
Sheriff elect of London and Middlesex, has
resigned through illness. Mr. Frederick Per-
kins, of London. and Southampton, is the only
candidate.

A female servant at Camden-house, Chisel-
burst, was, in company with a young man
named Croft, charged at the Mansion. house on
Saturday with having stolen a £',2o Bank of
England note, the property of the Emperor
Napoleon. His Majesty having missed several
notes of this value, communicated with the
police, and on Friday afternoon the male pri-
soner tendered one of them to a firm of
clothiers in the City in payment for a coat.
On inquiry at the Bank of England it was
found that the note had been stopped, and
both Croft and the young woman who accom-
panied him were taken into custody. In a box
belonging to the female prisoner five £2O notes
were afterwards found. They were both
handed over to the custody of the Kent
police.

At Belfast Police-court on Saturday Mr.
John Rea was again committed for seven days
for contempt of court. Mr. Rea was defend-
ing the driver of the carriage in which he was
conveyed on Thursday. The prisoner, who is
charged with assulting Sub-Inspector French,
refused to be represented by Mr. Rea. A
scene ensued. Mr. 111Isa1 when committed,

threw himself down, end was carried out of
court by the police.

A supplement to the London Gazette was
published on Saturday containing regulations
with reference to the rinderpest which has
recently broken out in the West Riding of
Yorkshire.

According to the Correspondencia of Madrid,
meetings are to be held there, at Barcelona,
Seville, and other chief towns, to procure the
abolition of slavery in Cuba. Numerous peti-
tions to that effect will be presented to the
Cortes at the opening of the session.

Two wife-beaters were brought up before
the magistrate at the Thames police-court on
Saturday, and each of them were sentenced to
two months' imprisonment with hard labour.
At Clerkenwell an offender of a similar cha-
racter was sentenced to four months of the
same punishment.

Inquests have been opened upon the bodies
of the five persons who were killed in the
explosion of gunpowder at Hounslow. In
eaeli case the evidence was confined to the
purposes of identification only, and the in-
quiries were adjourned.

On Saturday morning a large mill belonging
to Messrs. George Knowles and Sons, Bolton,
containing 32,000 spindles, was burnt to the
ground, and completely destroyed. The damage
is estimated at 1,35,000, which is fully covered
by insurance. Upwards of 200 hands are
thrown out of employment.

According to the North 619111(111 Gazette
the Bishop of Fameland has pAitioned the
Emperor for permission to present an addres.s
at Martenberg to his Majesty -attesting his
loyalty.
.The Emperor replied that be can
only receive the address on the Bishop declar-
ing himself to the fullest extent obedient to
the laws of the Empire.

On Monday, at Dunrobin, her Majesty
gracefully took part in the ceremony of laying
the foundation stone of the monument to the
late Duchess of Sutherland.

The Journal (1' Illustration has been seized
on the Boulevards by the police, on account of
it containing a drawing representing the con-
scription in Alsace, where Prussian soldiers
are seen tearing off the numb,lrs and favours
which the young men placed on their hats,
according to custom, in drawing the fortunate
numbers.

The express train from
.Barcelona to
Valencia was upset by, a land-slip of nearly a
mile in extent at 2.30 p.m. on Monday.
Many of the passengers were killed, amongst
whom was General Smith. Senator General
Audia was saved. The accident occurred on
sandy soil, between Tarragona and Tortosa.
Details are still wanting, in consequence of
the interruption of the telegraph between
Vinaroz and Tortosa.

Cruelly slow in its progress and oppressive
in its personal bearing on the prisoner, the
investigation of the charges against Marshal
Bazaine still gives no immediate promise of
result. According to the Courrier de France,
the inquiry has already revealed "criminal
intrigues compromising some important per-
sonages in connection with the capitulation of
Metz."

Friendly explanations having been inter-
changed between the Governments of France
and Italy, the former has given orders that no
further progress shall be made with certain
engineering works at the Col de Fregus, near
the Mont Cenis Tunnel, by which it was
intended to secure the territory of France from
any hostile use of the line in case of war.

Trouville, with its recreations in artillery
and philosophy, has benefited the health of
the President of the French Republic so much
that his best friends declare him never during
the past ten years to have looked as well as he
does at present. He is expected to return to
Paris about the 20th inst., and to stay in the
capital for some time. A correspondent re-
ports that the negociations with respect to the
Commercial Treaty with England are believed
to be going on very favourably, and that
the French Ambassador at the Italian Court
is expected home with important despatches.

On the Spanish frontiers a fresh outbreak
of the Carlist insurrection is hourly appre-
hended, if indeed it has not already taken
place; and the French Government—which
has of late shown itself so very conciliatory
and assiduous towards that of King Amadeus,
as if the old alliance might be renewed with
advantage—has taken all precautions to
arrest the insurgents, oven the august but
very little endangered person of Don Carlos
himself, should they try to take refuge north
of the Pyrenees.

A few days ago Mr. Arthur Kinnaird, M.P.,
was received by Prince Bismarck in Berlin as
the bearer of an address strongly condemning
the dogma of Papal infallibility, and expressing
sympathy and praise in relation to the Prince's
ecclesiastical policy, and a hope that Europe
will soon be freed from the pernicious influence
of Ultramontanism. This document is signed
by the Marquis of Cholmondeley, the Marquis
of Westminster, the Earl of Bandon, the Earl
of Dalhousie, 21 members of the House of
Commons, the Bishops of Worcester and
Ripon, and the President of the Wesleyan
Methodist Conference and many other dis-
tinguished ministers of religion.

The now tramways, called the Commercial -
road branch, which run between the East
India Docks and the previously existing line
at Whitechapel, joining it at the top of
Leman-street, were opened on Monday morn-
ing. Several handsome and commodious cars,
similar to those plying on the other lines of
this company, wore running throughout the
day, and from the excellence of the traffic and
the popularity of tramways in the neigh-
bourhood, it is „ expected that this branch will
prove a very lucrative addition to the com-
pany's system.

The first municipal election in Yarmouth
since the passing of the Ballot Act took place
on Monday. About half the electors voted,
and there Wftg an entire absence of the ex-
citement and disorder hitherto seen at
municipal elections. The Conservatives had
men to mark off on the register the name of
each voter as he came out of the booth, thus
enabling thenk. to know who had voted and
who had abstained from voting. They also
published an imaginary state of the poll at
ten o'clock, giving their candidate a majority
of 33. The poll closed at four o'clock, and
the votes were immediately counted, the re-
sult being that the Conservative was elected
by a majority of 2.14.

Galignani says that the operation of weigh-
ing the live hundred million francs just sent
by the French Government to Germany lasted
three days.

From New York we hear that Forrester, the
suspected murderer of the banker Nathan, has
been arrested.

The Council of the South of England Lite-
rary and Philosophical Society have just
passed a resolution expressing regret at the
proposed destruction of the Celtic fortification
at Wimbledon known as " Caesar's Camp," and
calling upon the Government to support Sir
John Lubbock's "National Monuments 13111"
next session.

. A singular ease was heard before the Ham-
mersmith police magistrate on Monday.
Harriet Weedon, a single woman in service,
placed her female child, 15 months old, under
the care of one Sarah Ann Rodwell, who lived
with a carman named Spaull as his wife.
During Rodwell's temporary absence from the
house, the child became cross, and Spanll, by
way of quieting it, administered a quantity of
pepper. The little creature died, and Spanll
is now in custody on a charge of having caused
its death. He has been remanded without
bail.

In a charge of wife-beating which was in-
vestigated at the Clerkenwell Police-court on
Monday, an exemplary sentence was passed,
the prisoner having been ordered to undergo
six months' imprisonment, with hard labour,
and to find a surety for his good behaviour
during half a year after his release.

There was an anti-Licensing Act demonstra-
tion in Oxford on Saturday night. The dis-
contented Oxonians assembled in High-street
just after the public-houses closed at eleven
o'clock, and remained there for two hours
denouncing the Licensing Act and singing
" Rule Britannia!' They afterwards smashed
th.e windows of a leading teetotaller, and when
threatening to attack the house of Alderman
Randall, who is strongly in favour of the early
closing of public-houses, were interfeted with
by the police, and a number of broken heads
was the result of the encounter. The dis-
turbances were renewed on Sunday night,
when the houses were closed at ten. At Read-
ing, on Monday, six men were fined for parti-
cipation in licensing riots on Saturday night.

On Monday evening an inquest was held at
Bath on the body of Miss Courteney, an
aged maiden lady, sister of the late Admiral
Courteney, who died in a cottage on the out-
skirts of this city in a wretched condition.
Though possessed of ample means she occupied
a half-furnished room, and slept on a couch
without changing her day clothes. An old
soldier brought her food twice a week, and
another man carried her wood and coal, but
neither entered her apartments. She was
found in a state of delirium, her only cover-
ing being a ragged chemise and an old
blanket. The stench of the room was un-
bearable. She had a sister in Bath whom she
would never sec. A verdict of "Death from
natural causes '' was returned.

Tho Right Hon. John Bright, M.P., has
been staying for a short time at Clifton,
being on a visit to his sister-in-law, Miss
Priestman. He is accompanied by Mrs.
Bright, and both attended the meeting of the
Society of Friends, at Rosemary-street, on
Sunday morning. He looks well, though he
does not appear quite so stout as on some
former occasions. Considerable interest was
evinced at his unexpected presence among the
Friends, and he received hearty congratula-
tions from those more intimately acquainted
with him. Mr. Bright has returned. to Roch-
dale.

The police have commenced a raid on the
public-houses in the suburbs of the metropolis,
which have hitherto done literally a "roaring
trade" on Siuiday morning; and the pro-
prietors of the Old king's Head tavern, on the
banks of the river Lea, and of the White Lion
in Hackney Wick, have been fined for this
offence, the magistrate remarking that the
man who merely goes out for a walk cannot be
called a bona fide traveller within the mean-
ing of the new Licensing Act.

A violent assault upon a policeman was
on Monday punished by the Clerkenwell
magistrate by a month's imprisonment, with-
out the option of a fine. Another similar
offender was ordered to pay a penalty of X 5.
At Greenwich an attack upon a constable
was visited with a sentence of two months'
hard labour. At the Lambeth Police-court
sentences of six weeks' hard labour were passed
upon three persons for this class of offence.

The Belfast News Letter says it has authority
for slitting that Sir Richard Wallace is now
the undisputed owner of the Hertford estates.
The matter was finally settled. in Loudon last
week.

sented will probably issue a Circular Note,

The Bombay mail arrived on Sunday.
Amongst other items of intelligence is the
death of Prince Oholam Mahomed, son of
Tippoo Sultan, and Chief of the Mysore Princes,
at the age of 78. Cholera is reported to be
prevalent at Bombay as well as at Simla, and
in many parts of the North-West. The su.rn
subscribed at Calcutta for Mrs. Elson, the wife
of the heroic pilot, who perished in a cyclone
under circumstances recently made public,
already amounts to about 6,000 reals.

Vesuvius appears to be giving premonitory
intimation of another eruption. Shooks have
been felt—only slight hitherto, however
near the mountain, and smoke is being emitted
from two of the craters.

M. Thiers's Government continues to repress
political demonstrations. The prefects have
been informed that banquets are not to be
allowed to celebrate the anniversary of the
Republic on the 21st or 22nd of September.;
the dates for which M. Gambetta declared hte
preference over the 4th. In taking th!s
course the Ministry point out that their
object is impartiality towards all political
factions, and a determination to maintain
peace and tranquillity—" necessary under
present circumstances."

On Sunday afternoon, the American yacl.t
Sappho, while cruising off the Isle of Wright,
ran ashore at Sandhead, about a mile from
Ryde. The next morning she was floated,
not having received any severe injuries, and
lies at her moorings, in Cowes Roads.

Several cases of rapid deterioration in the
copper or metal sheathing of her Majesty's
ships having recently been brought to the
notice of the Admiralty, orders have been
given that in future tho copper or metal
sheathing of every ship rrovided with it is to
be examined once in six months by divers, or
by docking, if such a course is considered
desirable and is practicable. Reports stating
the defects discovered, and steps taken to
remedy them, are to be transmitted to the
Admiralty.

It is thought probable that Father Ilya.-
einthe's marriage will be followed by that of a
large number of French priests, many of
whom are, according to the Patrie, going to
renounce publicly their vows of celibacy. The
average number of priests in France who
marry is, it appears, not less than from 20 to
30 a year.

On Sunday morning Divine service was
again performed in the English church at
Geneva by the Rev. H. Downton. The chapel
was crowded, and it is hoped that the scandal
connected with the dismissal has terminated.

The Swiss 'village of Zernet z, in the Canton
Grisons, consisting of 120 houses, was totally
destroyed last Friday by fire.

The annual regatta at Margate tool( place
on Monday, and late as it came hi the season,
its various aquatic contests were carried on
with much spirit.

The Emperor of Germany went on Mon-
day morning with the Czar and the Emperor
Francis Joseph, the Cron Prince, all the
other Princes of the Royal House of Prussia,
and many illustrious personages now visiting
Berlin, by special train, to Staaken, to witness
some manwuvres against an imaginary
enemy. Luncheon was taken on the field.
In the evening there was a grand dinner at
the Imperial Palace.

The Registrar-General's abstracts of the
agricultural statistics of Ireland for 1872 show
a decrease in the acreage under crops of
134,915. The principal decline is in potatoes,
amounting to 66,632 acres; flax shows a
falling oil to the extent of 34,667 acres;
wheat, 16,262; oats, 14,323. Of unoccupied
land, including bog and waste, there are
4,253,975 acres. The, returns of live stook
show, an increase in horses of 2,650; cattle,
80,781 ; and sheep 2(1,682. There is a decreoe
in pigs of 236,037. The total estimated value
of live stock is .E 37,117,517 which exceeds
that of 1871 by ,D 282,781. The number of
emigrants in the first seven months of this
year were 5-1,995, being an increase over 1871
of 5,840. The Registrar remarks, that no
preceptible movement is visible in the methods
of tillage and cultivation, and complains of
the unchecked growth of weeds in almost
every part of the country.

It is said that King Almada°, in the speech
from the throne at the opening of the Spanish
Congress, intends to reiterate the affirmation
that he has no desire whatever to imp&se hitu-
self upon the country, and that he is ready to
withdraw at the first indication from the re-
presentatives of the nation.

The French Government, repl3ing to re-
presentations, has promised that no more
arrests shall be made in connection with the
Paris Commune, except in the case of the
leaders of the insurrection and persons pill

General Schenck, the American Minister at
London, together with his three daughters and
private secretary, v ho have recently been
travelling through the north of Scotland, paid
a visit on Monday to many of the more
interesting architectural and industrial sights
of Glasgow.

We learn from New York that the .A merlon
Government expects to learn the result of the
Geneva Arbitration on Saturday (to-day). It
also anticipates being apprised at the 'same
time that the San Juan Boundary question
has been decided in favour of the United
States.

The Committee of the Great Western and
Bristol and Exeter Provident Society have
announced that the profits arising from the
recent fete in Nuneham-park amount to the
large sum of X 1,250, which has been placed
to the credit of the Widow and Orphans'
Fund.

A representative meeting of Liberals of the
eight contributory boroughs of Flintshire was
held on Monday, at Mold, at which it was
decided to support Sir Robert Cnnliffe as the
Liberal candidate for the representation of the
county, in succession to Sir John Hanmer.

Two privates in the Royal Irish Volunteer
Rifles were on Monday charged with drunken-
ness and disorderly conduct at the South
Eastern Railway Terminus, London-bridge,
and each of them was fined 10s. At Green-
wich a case was heard in which a man, whilst
in a state of intoxication, had committed an
assault upon ,a porter at the Rotherhithe
Station of the East London Railway, and a
penalty of 40s. was inflicted.

Two youths were, on Monday, charged at
the Highgate Police-court with having wilfully,
set fire to a quantity of furze on Hlmpstead
Heath. One of them, 17 years of age, pleaded
that he was lighting his pipe with a luoifer
match, when his companion pushed him into
the furze. Each of the defendants was fined
45., with an intimation that if they were
brought up again for a similar offence they
would be sent to prison.

The christening of the infant daughter of
Prince and Princess Christian will, it is under-
stood, be solemnised next week at the Windsor
Groat Park Chapel, near Cumberland Lodge,
by the Rev. St. J. Blunt, chaplain to the
Queen and vicar of Old Windsor.

The Liverpool School Board have forwarded
a resolution to the borough magistrates in
favour of any measures to diminish the evil of
drunkenness, which they consider, from
practical experience, to be the great barrier
to elementary education.

The body of 'a girl named Schepmans, 19
years of age, was found a few days back in the
Scheldt, at Antwerp. She had been heard the
previous day to announce her intention of com-
mitting suicide, because "her mother had
accused her of wearing out her boots too
quickly."

"The estimated receipts," says the Z'atrie,
"for the Budget of the city of Penis, show a
deficit of ten millions for the first half of
1872."

It is stated that the recent "incident" be-
tween the French representative and the
Porte has been amicably arranged, and that
M. de Vogue returns to Constantinople im-
mediately.

The Royal Cornwall Regatta took place
on Monday :—Five yachts competed for the
Prince of Wales's eighty guinea cup, the
winner being the cutter Oimara. The
Commodore's fifty guinea cup, competed for
by four yachts, was won y the liyosotis, and
the third prize of £2O, competed for by three
yachts, was won by the Lizzie.

The Courrier de France announces that the
Republican General, Billot, will shortly be
appointed to the coramand of a provincial
military district.

The following advice dated Havana, Aug.
26, has been received: " The Voz do Cuba
continues to combat the proposed issue of
60,000,000 dols, of bonds. .A solution of the
financial problem of Cuba is as remote now as
ever. Railroad communication between Puerto
Principe and Neuvitas is uninterrupted, and
, trains are running regularly."

to the 31st ult. Referring to Central America,

vernment of Honduras declared, on the 27th
,-.1.11Y, General Medina and all those who aided

has also sent to recall in all haste Generals

As two young ladies, Miss Mary Davis and
Miss Mintorn, were bathing at St. Leonard's,
opposite Warrior-square, the former got out of
her depth, and her friend, seeing her danger,
sprung past the breakwater to save her, but
the current was too strong, and Miss Mintorn
was instantly carried out. to sea. It so hap-
pened that the usual bathing-woman was
absent, and the boatmen could scarcely swim
fast enongh. There was a cry of distress, and
a young gentleman, jumping rapidly from the
Esplanade, took of his boots and coat, and
plunged into the raging water. The young
Lady could not be seen, but he watched till she
rose from the wave, and, seizing her by the
arm, held her above water till another man
and a boat, which had picked up Miss Davis,
reached them, and towed them all to shore.
The ladies were soon restored by stimulants
and friction, and the gentleman drove quickly
home. We hear his name is Lieutenant
Rerbert Napier Banbury, of the Royal
Artillery.

At Marlborough-street police court, on
Tuesday, a young Italian woman, who was
brought into court in such a state of health as
to draw from Mr. Newton a severe remark as
to the inhumanity of bringing her there at all
that day, was committed for trial for the
murder of her new-born infant, the body of
which, with the view of concealing it, she had
literally cut into fragments.

A special court of Common Council has
been summoned for Monday next at three
o'clock, at which a petition will be presented
from Mr. Edward Brooko, recently elected a
sheriff of London, praying to be relieved from
the obligation of serving in that capacity, hi
consequence of illness. The prayer of the
petition is sure to be granted, and a day will
then be appointed for a fresh election by the
Livery.

On Monday the annual distribution of
prizes took plaec in St. Stephen's School,
Westminster. The Rev. F. Shepherd mu
-
pied the chair. Mr. Buakmaster delivered an
address urging the necessity of constant per-
severing work. The science and art classes
in •connection with the schools, which are
better known as the Baroness Burdett•Coutts
Schools, are now in full operation, and are
well attended by the young men of the neigh-
bourhood.

The New York, _Herald of August 31 con-
tains a grateful acknowledgment of the letter
of thanks addressed in the name of the Queen
of England to the discoverer of Dr. Living.
stone, Mr. Stanley, and alludes also to the gift
of a gold snuff-box studded with diamonds
which accompanied the verbal recognition.
"The letter,' it is retnarked, though "short
and formal, as such notes usually are, breathes
a warmth and fulness of grateful feeling which
no stiff official phrasing can obliterate, and is
creditable alike to the Englishwoman and the
Queen." "We rejoice," the Herald adds,
"at the appearance of this generous tribute to
American pluck and enterprise."

Pilgrimages to various shrines have for
some time formed a marked feature in the
religious and social aspect of France. A
grand national pilgrimage is to take place on
the Bth of October, in the prospectus of which
it is declared that the Virgin has announced, in
"a vision," that she will manifest her power
in a grotto over a cave. The Ladies' Com-
mittee for this pilgrimage includes many of the
leaders of Frew% society.

A New York correspondent, speaking of the
prospects of the approaching Presidential
election, thinks that for the present Mr..
Greeley's progress towards the White House
has been checked; adding that for some days
there had been no new accessions to his aide,
and the tone of his supporters had changed
from exultation to subdued hopefulness. The
elections in the State of Maine have issued in
the return of all the five Republican candi-
dates for Congress. The Republicans have
also carried the election of all the State officers,
the members for the Senate, and four-fifths of
those for the House of Representatives.

Attention is being directed, now that coal
is becoming so dear, to the supply which may
be obtained from Ireland. Lough Allen, in
the county of Leitrim, about nine miles from
Carrick-on-Shannon (a station on the Midland
Great Western Railway), is surrounded on
three sides by mountains, all of which contain
mineral deposits, and, for many years, coal
obtained from these mountains has been
burnt in the village of Drumshambo and the
town of Carrick.

On Tuesday the coroner's jury returned at
Wolverhampton a verdict of manslaughter
against Gough, the man alleged to have killed
his wife by knocking her down after she had
returned from Wolverhampton races. The
post-mortem showed that the woman's neck
was fractured, and that a stocking needle,
used to fasten up the chignon worn by the
deceased, had penetrated the situ 1 to the ex-
tent of an inch,

Hannah Wilton and John Crofts, both
young persons, were charged at Sideup Petty
Sessions with stealing £l4O, belonging to the
Emperor Napoleon. The female prisoner was
a servant at Camden House, Chislehurst,
during the Emperor's residence there, and
had managed to get possession of the money,
consisting of £2O bank-notes, and secrete it in
her box. Crofts kept company with the girl,
by whom she is now enceinte; but it was
clearly proved that he had no knowledge of
the robbery. As £l2O of the sum had been
recovered, his Majesty recommended her to
mercy, at the same time requesting the
Justices to deal with the case summarily.
Crofts was discharged, and Wilton was sen-
tenced to three months' imprisonment.

The election of the new Lord Mayor is
fixed for the 28th inst., Michaelmas Day this
year falling on a Sunday. The first on the
list of candidates is Sir Sydney Waterlow, the
second Mr. Andrew Lusk, MP.; the third,
Mr. .D. H. Stone; the fourth, Mr. W. J. It.
Cotton ; the fifth, Mr. Thomas Owden. In the
event of the usual course of events being
carried out at the next election, Alderman
Sir Sydney Waterlow will be Lord Mayor of
London for the year 1872-3.

Throughout the large towns of the United
Kingdom last week, the average mortality
was at the rate of 24 per 1,000, which was also
the average of Dublin and Glasgow. In
Landon it was again 19, and in Edinburgh 18.
The most serious epidemic in the metropolis is
whooping-cough, from which there were 32
deaths. The births were 2,190 and the deaths
1,236. Deaths from violence numbered 39 in
all, and included two murders, four suicides,
and six fatal street accidents.

It is stated in a telegram from Madrid that
the deficit in the Spanish Budget which the
projected new loai is intended
,to cover
amounts to 2,600 millions of reals.

A few days ago a fearful crime was com-
mitted at the village of Ergisch, district of
Loecho, Valais. In a moment of rage, caused
by drunkenness, a young man killed his
father by stabbing him" with a knife. The
father, feeling his end to be nigh, caused his
son to be brought before him, when he forgave
him what be had done, pointed out to him the
surest means of escape, gave him some money,
and expired a moment afterwards.

Complaint was made at the meeting of the
City Commission of Sewers on Tuesday tha
the Great Eastern Railway Company had pro-
ceeded to bleak up Sun-street, one of the
most important thoroughfares in the City.
It was explained that the attempt of the Cor-
poration to restrain the company had failed
before the Lords Justices, and that the railway
authorities had therefore a legal right to close
the street. At the same time an appeal was
pending before the House of Lords, and if the
decision of the Court of Chancery should be
reversed, the company would be called upon to
reopen the thoroughfare and to pay conse-
quential damages.

Miss Rachel Bruce, second daughter of the
Home Secretary, was married on Tuesday to
Mr. Augustus G. Vernon Hareourt, eldest son
of Admiral Harcourt. The ceremony took
place at St. Margaret's district church,
Mountain Ash, Glanxorganshire, near Duffryn
House, the seat of Mr. Bruce.

Ten years' penal servitude was awarded at
Middlesex Sessions to a stonemason twenty-
two years of age, who had already received two
similar sentences of four and seven years re-
spectively, and had numerous other convictions
recorded against him. His crime on this
occasion was the theft of a coat.

For representing themselves falsely and
fraudulently to be Government Inspectors
under the New Licensing' Ad, and thus
endeavouring to procure liquor from a publi-
can, William Higham and Charles Thomson
were -fined 40s. each at Bow-street Police...
court; the offence being aggravated by inso-
briety at the time.

M. Thiers, from whose holiday doings at-
tention has been of late much distracted,
received on Tuesday the French Ambassador
at the Pupal Court, and went the next day
from Trouville to Val Richer on a visit to M.
Guizot—acoompanied by the War Minister,
General do Casey.

General that the mean temperature of the
air last week at the Royal Observatory, Green-
wich, was 64 deg. 5 min., and 6 deg. 2 min.
above the averap for the corresponding week
in 50 years. A considerable excess prevailed
on each of the days except Sunday, Ist; the

was 69 deg. 5 min., and 11 deg. 1 min, above

rain was measured in London, while in the

fell; in Manchester the fall amounted to two
inches and a half.

It is said that the repairs to the Glatton,
necessitated by the gun praolice at her turret,
will not amount to more than £3,500, includ-
ing the docking charges.

Eight immense boilers supplied by Messrs.
Rothwell, and put up at ?Woolwich in the new
boiler-house adjacent to the foundations laid
for the great 30-ton hammer, have been set
to work regularly, and the arrangement
appears to be very satisfactory.

Two cases of aggravated assaults upon
women were dealt with by the Westminster
Police Magistrate ou Tuesday, and sentences
of six and four months' hard labour were
respectively passed.

For an assault upon two policemen, a
labourer was sent to prison for two months by
the Marylebone magistrate. At Hammer-
smith, a similar offence was visited with four
months of the like punishment.

The Warrington Guardian announces the
arrival of 80 Jesuits at Ditton-hall, near War-
rington, a spacious residence placed at their
disposal as a home, and for educational pur-
poses by Mrs. Stapleton, of Rainhill.

The Czarowitch and the Prince of Wales are
expected in Paris early in October, when a
series of fetes will be given in their honour
at the Elyse.

The Rappel states that Austria and Spain
have protested against the right of the French
Government to impose a fixed duty of 10e. per
package for merohandizo in barrels, cases, or
bales, and a duty of 100. per 1,000 kilogrammes
of merchandize not in bales.

The Pennon authorities have arrested a
French subject, residing at Nancy, accused
of activity in promoting the choice of Alsa-
tians and Lorrainors in favour of French
nationality.

In speaking of Father llyaointhe's marriage,
the .dvenir Natio,nal says :—" We are in
position to affirm that Mrs. Merriman, the
widow to"whem ho is united, possesses a fortune
of 76,000 dols., that is to say, 375,000
francs."

Amongst other items of election intelligence,
it may be stated that Mr. Paul Isaac, a colliery
proprietor, of Colwick-hall, has consented to
contest Nottingham, in response to a requisi-
tion signed by more than 4,000 electors.. Mr.
E. Mileage will come forward as a Liberal
candidate for Mid-Lincolnshire, in succession
to Colonel Arocotts, who intends to retire.

A full acquittal of both the accused has
been the result of the trial at Brest of the
Jesuit Father Dufour and the Viscountess de
Valmont, who were charged with scandalous
conduct in a railway carriage.

The "Festival of the Three Choirs" began at
Worcester on Tuesday with special service in
the Lady Chapel—the musical part of which
seems to have been indifferently 'performed.
"Elijah" was given in the Cathedral at noon, to
a brilliant and numerous audience, with per-
fect eflioiency and success.

Two passenger trains and a luggage train
came into collision at Snow-hill Junction, on
the London, Chatham, and Dover branch line
from Ludgate-hill to Farringdon-street, on
Tuesday morning. Except to rolling stock,
no injury was done ; an empty first class
carriage was broken:up, while the next saloon,
which was occupied by a family, escaped with-
out a scratch.

The importation of coal from Belgium goes
on briskly at Grimsby. The exporters at that
town give it as their opinion that the price of
coal has now reaohed its maximum. •

From April Ist to the 7th inst. the national
income amounted to £29,093,037, as compared
with £26,837,154 in the corresponding period
of last year. The expenditure has been
£31,042,295, and t'lis alto was an increase
upon the sum expended in the same time
twelve months ago. On Saturday last the
balance in the Bank of England exceeded four
millions and a half sterling.

Marseilles has been the scene of an accident
which those who detest and condemn the
brutal practice of bull-fighting may think to
happen only too seldom, as a punishment to
the spectators. A bull sprang over the barrier
of the arena, and rushed furiously among the
crowd, injuring many of them before its career
could be stopped by a mortal thrust from a
soldier's bayonet. The confusion was en-
hanced by the escape of the other bulls.

dates in both cases being chosen, while the

We are not answerable for the opinions expressed by our

to the Editor of the BEE-Ilivs. Those who desire their

our space is so limited, and on one side of the paper

THE MASONS AND JOINERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sra,—Permit me to say, in reply to Mr.
Scott, and for the future benefit of trades
unionists generally, that the real difference
'between the masons and joiners in their late
dispute was in their respective modes of pro-
beading in order to effect a settlement. The
masons, to their credit, promptly, and for the
first time in the history of the Society, so far as 1
hnow it, empowered their delegates to "nego-
tiate discretionally " with their employers.
The result of that negotiation was, and is,
highly satisfactory--they gained much, and
lost nothing. At the worst they could but
have gone in on the old terms, and that would
have been better than a protracted strike with
consequent demoralization of the union locally,
and the creation of a multitude of opposi-
tionists. The joiners, on the other hand,
would not empower their delegates to nego-
tiate diseretionally, hence the strike on their
part has been protracted until their eontidence
was sufficiently spurred to induce them to con-
cede the point of "discretional negotiation"
which the employers wisely and justly insisted
upon when the strike terminates, I hope as
much to their satisfaction as did that of the
masons to the satisfaction of the latter.

This want of confidence in one another, and
particularly in their best men, by trades
unionists, which has led thorn so tardily to
adopt the principle of "discretional negotia-
tion" in their disputes with their employers,
hns caused scores of thousands of pounds to be
sr:pandered ruthlessly and, uselessly, and in-
flicted immense privation and distress upon
workmen, their wives and families. London,
is, however, •at last inaugurating a., better
way.
Whatever "understanding may have existed
between the masons anti the joiners relative to
the recent "strike or lock-out," they must
,have regarded as their ultimate end a speedy
and satisfactory settlement with the employers,
and if one division of the army of labour sue-
ceeded in gaining a speedy and. decisive
Victory, it ought to have ,been a cause of
eneouragerdent and satisfaction to the other
divisions of the same army, instead of exciting
their pique and jealousy, which could only end
in spite against themselves. Fancy the army
of the North annoyed and mortified because
the army of the South gains a more speedy
and decisive victory at Worth. Under such
circumstances it is mere nonsense to talk of
one party acting traitorously towards the
other.

The concluding paragraph of Mr. Scott's
letter contains a very uncomplimentary and
sad reflection Upon Messrs. Applegarth and
Cramer, whose personal differences are con-
sidered to be such as to incapacitate them for
giving sound and useful advice to their old
associates and fellow-workmen. It is a new,
but equally poor excuse for the egotism that
tie elcs to exclude from the couneils of trades
unionism the hest experienced and most
intelligent members, originally and ostensibly,
because' they are not now of the trade;
now because they have personal differences,
really because those who are of the trade
possess too high an opinion of their own
competency. Let by-genes be 'by-genes, and
let us hope that conceit will abate, jealousy
cease, differences be reconciled, and that ere
long a bettor way will be found which will
obviate strikes and lock-outs altogether.—
Your's respectfully,
Bolton, Sept. 2nd, 1872.

articles.title: STANDING ARMIES AND THE WORK-
articles.text:
STANDING ARMIES AND THE WORK-

ING CLASSES.

To the Editor of' the BEE-HIVE.

Srn,—Few things are more easy than to
argue certain principles from one's own point
of view. The controversialist may then in-
dulge in all his own pet theories without
noticing opposite truths or principles. Hence
we often see men writing in our public journals
the most astounding fallacies, and making them
appear correct and reasonable.
The author of the article upon "Standing
Armies" in last week's BEE-HIVE is no doubt
well acquainted with the subject he took in
hand. .He very truly states that the masses
have not awoke to a sense of the important
trust and responsibility which has devolved
upon them. Whether war and standing
armies is a subject upon which working men
seldom think or are indifferent about, is a
question upon which there will be a diversity
of opinion. That maintaining standing
armies is a disgrace upon the world's civiliza-
tion few will deny. It is one of the most
painful and disheartening thoughts to the
lover of humanity and progress, that we are
now in possession of weapons of war calculated
to kill more men in a shorter time than in any
previous period of the world's history, and I
feel quite certain that most people will agree
that it is a pity that so many able-bodied men
are trained up for the special purpose of kill-
ing each other. Looked at from one point of
view, it is amazing that it is still permitted,
and, so much hard-earned money spent upon
, it. But do not those who are so loud in their
oondemnation of it, and so' anxious for us to
abolish our army, take a very one-sided view
of the whole question? It is very easy indeed
to write about the cost and inconvenience of
our standing army, but I have never yet seen
any sensible remedy for the evils complained of.
Are we, in the presentstate of Europe and the
world, to abolish all our means of defence, and
trust to chance for the future? Are we to
rely upon providence and. the , magnanimity of
our Continental neighbours to make and keep
our, island secure? Is it not a well-known
fad that nothing but the "British Lion" pre-
vents some of the military monarchies of the
Continent from encroaching upon our Pro-
perty and possessions. I believe the majority
of Englishn2en are averse to war, and would
gladly avail themselves of any means by which
it might be prevented. But who will dare to
say the same of the French, the Prussians, the
Russians, or even the Austrians and Turks.?
Would they, if we at once laid down our
arms, applaud our motives, and look upon
England and her possessions as sacred? I
fear not, and. am inclined to believe that there
is avarice and ambition sufficient amongst
them to take advantage of any of our weak
parts. Looking at the present strength of
Russia and Prussia, and the preparations of
France, we have not yet arrived at that time
when it would be prudent to "turn our
swords into ploughshares." Our army is a
necessity—a 'dreadful necessity, a deplorable
necessity, but it is a necessity.
It might be asked what is the use of all our
police forces, and why do we not abolish them
and thus save tho expense? The answer is they
are necessary for the prevention of crime and
the preservation of property. In the same
light we regard our army and navy.
We do not look upon them with delight,
but we maintain them in order to preserve
our own existence and security. Such being
the case, it is wise that we endeavour to make
them as perfect as possible' in order to keep
them as small as possible. We have an em-
pire upon which the sun never sets, yet how
few of oven the small kingdoms of the Con
tinent have so small an army as ours. And
as to the autumn manomvres, to which objec
tion is made on the ground of expense, it is
not necessary to defend them if we are to
have an army at all. Perhaps some who are
loud in complaints about the expense would
prefer fifty times the amount being spent
in a real war caused by our not being pre-
pared for an enemy. In conclusion the
arguments of the peace party would suit
very well for the world as it ought to be,
but they fail to fulfil the requirements
of the world as it is.

W. BRUCE.
Heekmondwike, September 12th.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

The -iticia-0--on thissubject, contained, in
your last number, and signed by Mr. IL M.
Latham, very aptly illustrates what is :called
the apathy of the working classes on political
questions; for the cause of this apathy we have
not far to seek.

The fault does not lie with the working
classes, but in the subjects. The object of Mr.
Latham is to enlist the operatives on the side
of those who declaim against the institution of
a standing army, on the ground that the
taking of so many men from the productive
industries of tho country is a serious loss to
the: nation.
Unfortunatley for the success of his applica-
tion, his doctrine runs counter to the common-
sense feeling of the classes to ix,horn he appeals.
It is useless to attempt to fuddle them with
dogmas of political economy; they feel, they
know, that to throw the men, now employed
in the army, upon the labour market, would

be adverse to their interests; would reduco
their wages, would replace them under that
bondage to the capitalist from which they are
now struggling to get free.
Even that unfortunate conspiracy against
the interests of the toiling millions—political
economy—admits as much. It tells us, with
the most unflagging reiteration, that the more
there are to divide, what it styles the "labour
fund," the less wages there must be for
each.

But these advocates of the capitalist interest
urge that these armies are kept in idleness at
a great expense to the tax-payers, and they
would insinuate, though they might avoid say-
ing in so many words, that the funds for this
purpose were extracted mainly from the work-
ing classes. Let us examine the amount of
truth contained in such an argument.
Last year the total revenue exceeded 7i
millions, of which stamps, income and pro-
perty tax, licenses, house and other assessed
taxes, telegraphs, &c., not contributed to by
the working man, exceeded 25 millions, leaving
less than 50 millions to be provided by
Excise, Customs duties, Post-office, and mis-
cellaneous sources.

Now, assuming that one half of these 50
millions, and surely that will be admitted to
be a fair proportion, were paid by the working
portion of the population, that would show
that two-thirds of the army is maintained by
those classes not belonging to the operative
classes.

Last year the army cost more than 16
millions, of which two-thirds, or 10 millions,
were provided by the upper classes-10
millions, which were spent almost exclusively
in giving employment to those who provide food,
clothes, shelter, (U., for our military forces.
Let us deduct two millions from that sum for
the profits of the contractors, and other items,
all of which, however, excepting what might
be saved and invested in foreign loans, would
eventually pass through the hands of the
artisans and labourers. This leaves eight mil-
lions spent annually, almost directly, in paying
wages. Now, assuming that the wages of men,
women, and children, thus employed., averaged
£1 per week, or £.50 per annum, we find that
the institution of our standing army gives
employment to 160,000 individuals, and besides
that, keeps 800,000 able-bodied men out of the
labour market.
Is this the sort of "Root Question" on
which the wage-receiving classes are likely to
cease to be apathetic?
Working men's polities, to possess any
vitality, must spring naturally and directly
out of working class interests. Those who
aspire to lead them must shun the closet-spun
theories of amateur political economists, and
take their stand upon practical wants, and
common sense.

PRIESTORAFT.
To the Editor of the BEE-HivE.

Sin,—ln an article on priests and govern-
ments it is said of priests "They'll die of
themselves if you let them alone," and it
assumes that they are hypocrites and counter-
feits, whom all honest men should wish dead.
But the Established Church at home ,is
claiming, through its bishops and priests, to
be the Catholic Church; and thus the con-
demnation of the Catholic priests abroad is a
condemnation of Catholic priests at home who
claim to be in union and communion, and
when men are known to be hypocrites and
counterfeits, are they to be established by the
people with millions upon millions of national
inoome to save them from dying out? Why,
surely, if men were to forgo counterfeit
sovereigns, the people of an honest nation
would never endow the forgers with millions
upon millions annually in order to enable
them to maintain a mint in every parish
'throughout the kingdom, where they might
manufacture and pass off these counterfeits?
And, surely, the people of an honest nation
would never be a party to enable the forgers
to stamp their counterfeit coins with •the
national coat-of-arms, so that the forged coins
might pass cutrent as the nation's? And,
surely, whilst forgers were thus endowed and
established, it would be absurd to suppose
that "they would die of themselves if let
alone." Nay, nay; the nation that tolerated
such baseness would perish first; and, there-
fore, if the nation would not fall as France
has, let the people disestablish the Catholic
priests as false stewards who have appro-
priated the wealth and name of a Protestant
nation to convert our Church into a Catholic
Church, and pass it off on the people as the
English Church.
And it is as much the duty and the interest
of the people to prevent counterfeit doctrines
passing current "an national ones," as it is
their duty and interest to prevent counterfeit
sovereigns passing current as national ones.—
I am, dco.,
Petersham, S.W.

T. G. HEADLEY.

TUE CARPENTERS' AD JOINERS AND
THE MASONS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
Sia,—Being a constant subscriber to the
BEE-HivE, and an. admirer of its principles,
and a member of the present mnoh-maligned

branch of the building trades, I beg leave to
offer a few remarks on the late dispute. Now,
air, I would have everyone write what he
knows, and as much as he knows, but no more.
Your correspondent, Mr. Mitehley, falls into
some grievous errors, and deviates very widely
from the truth, when he trusts to a dim and
hasty recollection of prior events, and on the
present occasion he says that the masons have
made dishonourable terms, and not geOd
enough for the carpenters and joiners. Per-
haps he will be kind enough to inform us what
part of the terms are dishonourable—is it the
wages part of the question, or the shorter
hours worked in the winter weeks?
I cannot see how to reconcile what has been
said and written by the carpenters and joiners
as to their motives for adopting the nine hours
movement—viz., to put more men into em-
ployment and the terms they have made,
refusing to accept the same hours as the
masons, and agreeing to work 5,1 hours more
per week at the dullest season of the year
when the greatest number are out of employ-
ment, and, when, according to their professed
motives, there is the greatest need for work-
ing short hours. I see their delegates calcu-
late, under the revised scale for over-
time, to make 57-1- hours per week. So muoh
for professions and practice.
Mr. Scott, before he persists in calling US
traitors, will perhaps be kind, enough to answer
the following questions—When and where this
much talked-of agreement was entered into,
also,tif such agreement existed, why did the car-
penters and joiners strike two large firms, and
not consult the masons' committee? Then, _
again, when the employers offered to put the
questions at issue to arbitration when the
carpenter delegates met the master builders
and succeeded in postponing the look-out for
a few days, and agreed to meet them the fol-
lowing day to arrange the terms of arbitra-
tion, why not consult the masons? Had they
not as much right as the carpenters and
joiners to a voice in the question, seeing that
the masons' memorial had been before the
master builders folly two months before the
carpenters and joiners sent theirs? Was the
public press the most business-like way of
Informing the masons' committee of the steps
they were about to take of two bodies of men
that were acting in concert? If we are to
believe the statements of Messrs. Mitehley and
Scott, the masons had no knowledge of those
two Important events but what transpired
through the press. If your correspondents
will clear up those points, and give to the
world at large a true version of the spirit that
then animated the carpenters and joiners at
that time, we perhaps shall not have such
harsh terms applied to us by ignorant men.
Hoping you will give :this a place in your
next issue,—l remain, yours, &a

. A. CARE, Mason.
Berkhampsted, Sept. 4th.

THE BAKERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-lirvt.

Srn,—Eight years have now gone since last I
addressed yen on the Bakers' Short Time
Movement. In concluding a letter then to
your valuable paper, I breathed the wish
that the men would show that they
were brothers in the truest sense of the
term, and stand fast and immovable for the
hours, four to four, and no.surrender. 1, Sir, in
common with many others' rejoice to see that
there is soon likelihood of this happy consum-
mation at least, seeing that they have now
made their appeal to the public, without whose
help they were in a great measure powerless to.
attain those much needed wants of shorter hours
and larger pay. How painful to hear suolt
names again and again hurled at the bakery as
white slave, working in an often ill-ventilated,
dark and uninviting atmosphere of London
dirt and smoke, where often there is nothing
to be seen or heard but the continual patter
of the street passengers as they hurry to and
fro on their various missions of business.
Why, Sir, I ask, should such a state of mutters
be allowed to exist in the, metropolis of the
world? seeing that almost every member of
our toiling community has attained that
much needed object, viz., the shortening of the
hours of labour, and in most cases better
remuneration for their labour. A. few words,
Sir, and I have done for the present. Bakers
of London be firm, stand fast one to another,
and let your motto ever and anon be four to
four, and no surrender; let this be your every
day watchword and cry, and doubtless in the
end you will gain your just and reasonable
request. —I am, Sir, yours respectfully,

hifiS ROBiRTSON.
126, Prim ess-street, Dundee.

THE LABOURERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

you allow the following to appear.
in the next issue of your working men's
journal?
A labourer named Peach engaged to do
some harvest work by the acre for Mr. Core,
of this city, farmer, and when the man bad
done cutting, the foreman, named Cooper:
wanted to engage him to work by the day%
but Peach refused, and demanded to ha"
his work measured up, as he was going to
leave the neighbourhood for harvest elsewhore•
Cooper, however, refused to allow the surveyor

to come on the land, and said that he would
lave none measured, until the harvest was all
completed, and then he would have all measured
together. In vain Peach protested that he
should be away, and that he had a right to
be present at the measuting of his work, and
therefore it ought to be done at once. Cooper
refused, and the labourer had-to leave. ,Jri
returning home last week, he found the work
had been measured in his absence by Mr.
Core's surveyor, and, on looking over the
bills, he found that, in one •field at least, the
land was not so much, by more than an acre,
as he expected. He told the foreman so, and
insisted upon having his work re-measured.
On going down, however, with the surveyor,
the fore m an threatened to:kick him off the ground
if he wart on, and told him to get any more
money if he could. The bailiff also made some ob-
servations about Mr. Taylor, the president of the
District Labourers' Association here, which
Was neither polite or complimentary, and
Peach's connection with the society. As Mr.
Cooper handed the labourer over to Mr.
Taylor, be took his advice, and that gentle-
man at once put Peach in the way of seeing
himself righted. Another surveyor was taken,
and in spite of the foreman's remonstrance and
incivility, the ground-was again surveyed,
when it was discovered that there was an acre
and seven perches too little in the first
measure's account. On the farmer hearing this,
and no doubt expecting the labourer ;would
seek redress, he paid the extra money, amount-
ing to £1 Os. 7d. It was insisted that some
other man had got Peach's land measured to
him, and consequently Peach's money; be this,
however, as it may, on applying to the associa-
tion he was put in the way of obtaining that
which he appeared likely to lose, viz., a some-
what considerable portion of his hard-earned
harvest money, which to Peach would have
been a serious loss.—Yours obediently,
A MEMBER OF THE UNION.
Peterborough, Sept. 3rd, 1872.

A woman applied to the Salford magistrates
on Tuesday for advice as to how she could
regain possession of her daughter, a girl
aged 15, who, she said, "had been taken to
the Roman Catholic church and baptised."
The applicant alleged that the girl had been last
seen in company of some Sisters of Mercy, and
that a priest to whom she had applied had
told her "that if she allowed her daughter to
go to the Roman Catholic Church he 'would try
to find her." She declared that rather than
permit the girl to become a Roman Catholic
'she would die for her. The magistrate told
the applicant she could take her girl away by
force if she found her, but that the court
could do nothing until it was known where
the child was.

A distressing accident happened near Lang-
barn° Sands, in Carmarthen Bay, on Tuesday.
A party of gentlemen, amongst whom was Mr.
E. W. Greenwood, the vice-principal of the
South Wales Training College, went out on
a fishing exoursion. A squall arose and the
boat was capsized. All were excellent swim-
mers, but unfortuntaely Mr. Greenwood, who
belonged to Leeds, and the eaptain of the
boat were drowned.

A ease was heard at the Southwark Police
Court on Wednesday, in which a young
man employed in a loan and discount office
had attempted to take the goods of a bor-
rower under a bill of sale for an amount
considerably beyond the sum advanced. On
the man's wife resisting the process, the
defendant brutally assaulted her, for which
lie was sent to prison for two months by
Mr. Partridge, who denounced "these paltry
loan offices" as a "disgrace to the com-
munity."
